Messages.Author: madma...@my-deja.com
Messages.Body:
Hey, doesn't anyone write tournament reports here??

Tournament reports in this venue consist of only a relatively
lackluster list of finalists, the type of decks they played, and a
decklisting of the tournament winner.

Where's the drama? Where's the excitement? Where are the sneaky
plays, the last minute reprieves, the wild battles, the coups, the blow-
by-blow descriptions of pivotal battles??

I was disappointed to see just a few reports come out of Origins (and
then only after I primed the pump) and a complete lack of any coherent
description of the US Nationals at GenCon.

Now, perhaps I'm spoiled, coming from a Magic background where
tournament reports have developed into a fine art (although there are
some crude ones too [joke alert]). And I certainly admit I haven't
written anything up on GenCon either (my excuse being trying so hard to
stay alive [e.g. Hamblin as a predator and Churchill as a prey in the
Sabbat draft] that I neglect to remember what I did), but I will
endeavour to in the future.

IMHO, the drama, fun, and excitment of tournaments will help show V:tes
for the dramatic, fun, and exciting game that it is to all those
readers out there, compelling them to get off their rears and to join
us in our fun.

It doesn't have to be a major tournament or indeed any tournament -- it
could be a local playgroup. It just has to be fun.

Anyway, that's my rant for this month.

Yours,
Madman

Sent via Deja.com http://www.deja.com/
Before you buy.

Messages.Author: Joshua Duffin
Messages.Body:
In article <8nekb1$9kr$1...@nnrp1.deja.com>,

madma...@my-deja.com wrote:
> Hey, doesn't anyone write tournament reports here??
>

Ah, you're so right.

I only actually played in one Jyhad tournament
at GenCon (because I am a terrible terrible
failure and was late to both the Thursday
constructed and the Friday Sabbat draft - well,
I did play a couple games in the side-unsanctioned
tourney on Friday, but I sucked there too). And
I didn't take any notes (umm, of course I didn't,
because it's against the tournament rules...), but
here's what I can remember of the games.

I was playing Brujah pot/cel rush (of course).
Well, I say "of course", but I would have played
something else if I'd had anything else good to
play. I accidentally took my halfway decent
Nos/other Obf/Pot/Aus 5th/Minion Tap/Pulse/stealth/
combat deck apart a couple weeks before GenCon,
because I was tired of playing it, and then what
I ended up with were: (a) an all-Sabbat !Malk stealth
and bleed deck, which was not terrible but had very
poor combat and vote defense; (2) a fairly silly
mainly-Gangrel Ani/For deck with princes, 5ths,
Minion Taps, a pile of Drawing out the Beast, Dawn
Op, Skin of Steel, Amaranth, Ritual of the Bitter
Rose, Absolution of the Diabolist (it didn't work
very well for the obvious reason that if you didn't
block it it couldn't bleed you for more than about
two an action); (iii) a stupid presence-weenie deck
of 40% master cards, including a bunch of Anarch
Revolts, plus KRCs, ConAgs, Praxis Seizures, Third
Tradition - Progenies, Presence skill cards for them,
etc (this deck worked okay, except that it was always
the most obvious threat on the table and so it was
often immediately whacked); (d) the previously mentioned
Brujah (and !Bru, and Jimmy Dunn) pot/cel Rush deck,
which almost always kicks ass and takes names, but
is only rarely able to get many victory points.

So anyway, after seeing how much that DotB/Dawn Op
deck sucked when playing in the side games on
Friday, I decided to play the good old Brujah on
Saturday. (Good old rock. Nothing beats rock.)

First round, umm, I don't think I know any of the
players' names. My prey was playing a Tremere deck
with Cryptic Missions and dominate +bleed, looked
like mainly small vamps, he may have had Society of
Leopold in there but I never saw 'em. Grandprey was
playing I think a pre/obf stealth-bleed deck, which
was quite effective. Setites and others. Grand-
predator was playing an !Malk stealth-bleed deck,
which actually looked surprisingly similar to mine,
except that he seemed to have more Kindred Spirits
(I only have three, sadly). And my predator was
playing, umm, some kind of weenie presence vote deck
I believe. He made a bunch of princes early on,
starting with Antoinette DuChump, moving on to Delilah
Leaston, etc etc.

So my deck kinda choked at the beginning there; I failed
to draw the +hand damage and Grapples and Rushes all
at the same time, so my prey got set up with about five
princes in play and a couple Progeny and Embraces. But
he wasn't doing all that much damage to me yet at that
point; I dunno if he wasn't drawing KRCs and such or
didn't even have 'em in. So I was bleeding my prey for
a few, beating up his vamps once in a while, and trying
to beat up my prey's vamps sometimes. (Oh yeah, the
other reason I sucked is that my prey had Elysium the
Arboretum out, and the votes to defend it, and I ditched
a Rampage my first turn before I saw what he was playing.)

So the table was humming along for a while, I was doing
nothing much good but everyone else's deck seemed to be
working pretty well. The first major threat seemed to
be the stealth/bleed presence deck, since he was pretty
consistently bleeding the !Malks for three or so an action,
and !Malk guy was getting low on pool. I thought !Malk
guy should have gotten serious about trying to oust Pre-
weenie guy a little earlier, since Pre-weenie guy was
fairly low on pool already (didn't seem to have gotten
much pool gain). But when he finally did try it, he got
him down to about one or two and then rolled over and
died to the Pre bleeder, who naturally quickly followed
up by killing the weenie voter. So at that point I tried
to rush the stealth bleeder's guys into torpor, after
attempting to offer him a deal where I wouldn't kill his
vamps if he didn't bleed me for a turn or two (since I
thought I could oust my prey, who was also low on pool,
given that time). Sadly he saw right through me and
refused since if I did oust my prey he figured I would then
probably be able to take him down as well (which is exactly
what I was figuring, but I was hoping he wouldn't notice).
So I killed about one of his vamps and then he killed me
dead, and took the sweep.

Second round, my prey was Robyn (don't remember her last
name, sorry) playing a Minion Tap/5th Nosferatu-type
deck, plenty of stealth. Grandprey was Galen (again no
last name) playing a Gangrel intercepty sorta deck with,
apparently, a bunch of tricky stuff although I never saw
that part work too well. Grandpredator was, umm, don't
know his name, playing I think mostly-Ventrue bleed/vote?
Apparently had lots of combat defense (or at least he
said so). Predator was playing another 5th/Minion Tap
deck, although he never actually got out a Prince, and
so he died a horrible (though very slow) death to the
first turn Antediluvian Awakening he put out (which also
seemed to be a major destabilizing force on the table).

So. Robyn kept getting out Princes and Tapping them and
5thing them, none of which I could do anything about.
But pretty much whenever I desired, I could Rush one
of her vamps and put it in torpor empty. Problem was,
I didn't want to kill her *that* quickly, cause I
wanted her to put some pressure on Galen first. Other
problem was I was worried about staying alive against
my predator and that damn Awakening - he never got any
princes but he did bring out Cassandra - Optimagus Prime,
and later I think Rebekka - Chantry Elder of Frikkin'
Munich. So, she kept gaining pool *way* beyond what I
could bleed for, and I kept bleeding for three or four
a turn, and putting her princes in torpor when it seemed
necessary. When it all started getting real ugly, I tried
to talk Galen into trying to kill his prey, but he wouldn't
do it; apparently he was too worried about Robyn and my
predator walking away with the game with their 5th/Tap
thing (although my predator never really seemed able to
do anything in this game, Galen and his prey pegged him
and Robyn early on as the ones to watch, due apparently
to the 5thy stuff). So instead, my grandpredator killed
my predator, and then I tried to Rush his ass, but he
did indeed have some combat defense (lots of Majesty,
which of course was pretty useless against my Grapples,
but also some Skin of Steel, which slowed me down, and
I think he got an Elysium too, though I think I managed
to Rampage on that one), and so I died too when he got
to me and sent some +bleed my way. Robyn was still in
the game at that point, and I think she had just ousted
Galen (or was just about to) with her piles of stealth.
I don't know how the game turned out but I wouldn't be
surprised if Robyn did end up winning, if she got out
another replacement prince.

Third round, my prey was, umm, forgot his name, playing
Brujah pot/cel/dom combat/bleed/vote? Was definitely
playing the Wonder Twins, though he only got out one
(Constanza Vintner) to go with the Anvil he screwed me
out of (I had two blood on my Anvil when he brought his
up) and the Tura Vaughn who joined them later in the
game. Grandprey was Frederick Scott, playing a weenie-
horde thing with about a zillion Embrace, giving them
Fortitude and apparently Potence, with what seemed to be
the goal of preventing all your damage and Pulling your
Fangs, or Disarming you, or both. It looked like a good
plan, but having twelve minions out is a little too
obvious, and he was the first to go. Grandpredator was
playing a Giovanni deck with some intercept (Spectral
Divination I think?) and some combat and some bleed.
Predator was playing another 5th/Tap deck with Toreador;
Anson (Grunge Prince of Seattle) came out early and his
buddy Isabel de Leon bought him a ticket to the Toreador
Grand Ball so he could do his 5ths unentangled with us
lesser immortals. Later on Anneke showed up too.

In this game, I bled my prey a bit early on, and then
some more later, and some more after that, but it all
came to naught. I think it was my third turn that
my Dr. Dre, Chronic Leader of the Cold Dawn got superior
Potence and came over to bleed, getting blocked by that
traitorous Anvil. Testing the waters, you know. So
I ripped off a Signpost, so did he, I smacked him around
for about five and he smacked me around for about three,
and we both Tasted. Hmmm. So much for those waters.
So after that I bled when I felt like I had a good hand
of combat cards, and I hoped he would get himself down
to oust range by buying vampires. He nearly did, too,
except that he had a couple Wakes in there, and managed
to oust his prey (Mr. Scott and his horde of weenies)
with a second damaging vote that the table let him pass
(the first one was an Ancilla Empowerment that did about
nine to F. Scott; I didn't think it was a good idea to
get him killed, but I had no say since I only had about
one vote if that, and my prey had four and my predator
about five). So that put him out of range for me. At
that point I figured I was just about totally screwed;
I think I did something toward trying to keep my
predator down (up till that point he had been doing
essentially nothing to me - I don't think he'd even
bled me once, just fiddled with his 5ths and Taps and
masters and such), but it pretty much went nowhere what
with the Secure Haven and stuff. Oh yeah, and I had
contested Anvil when my prey was down to about two pool,
figuring he'd have to yield or get ousted (or yield *and*
get ousted, as I hoped), but instead he gained pool for
ousting his prey and I went to the land of suck. I paid
for Anvil for a couple more turns and got ousted somehow;
it was probably some damaging vote that my predator
called but I could be wrong. I was actually only half
paying attention to the game at that point (bad Josh,
I know) since I had just realized that I wasn't going
to really have any time to mess with my Shadowfist decks
before the Throne War finals started at 7, so I was taking
them out and fiddling with them during other people's
turns.

So then I was ousted, and that was my tournament, with
0 VPs in three rounds. (Obviously I did not make the
finals.) Boy, do I suck. I am like the suckiest suck
that ever sucked. Let me reiterate that next time, if
there is a next time, I will try to put more effort
into bringing along some decks that are actually good,
or at least that have some reasonable hope of getting
lots of victory points.

Josh

Messages.Author: Derek Ray
Messages.Body:
On Wed, 16 Aug 2000 17:51:39 GMT, madma...@my-deja.com wrote:

>Hey, doesn't anyone write tournament reports here??

And that's improved from a year ago. =)

>Where's the drama? Where's the excitement? Where are the sneaky
>plays, the last minute reprieves, the wild battles, the coups, the blow-
>by-blow descriptions of pivotal battles??

Well... you have to have a few things on hand before you can write a
dramatic report of the finals of a tournament, much less any
description of the rounds played.

First, you have to have someone there watching the whole finals and
paying attention, so's to actually remember things. Probably taking
notes. Players' viewpoints will tend to be a bit one-sided, although
that's better than nothing. This is a problem because most
non-finalists tend to leak away for pickup games at some point. =)

Second, that someone has to be capable of being eloquent enough to be
able to WRITE something dramatic, exciting, etc. Lets a lot of people
out.

Third, that someone has to understand the game well enough to
accurately describe the plays, read the players' intentions, and
provide an opinion on "good" or "bad" for the crucial plays. This
will make him unpopular, especially the first time he notes some "bad"
calls being made by players. (geez... it sounds like football.)

Fourth, someone has to be willing to do it, as well as the others.
Probably the most difficult thing out of all of them.

>Now, perhaps I'm spoiled, coming from a Magic background where
>tournament reports have developed into a fine art (although there are

I would be amazed that a Magic game could be written up as either
dramatic or exciting, but I suspect that's just my antiMagic bias
talking. =) I'd actually be somewhat surprised that a VTES game
could be written up as dramatic/exciting, but the multiplayer format
would provide for some additional cut-and-thrust, I suppose.

>some crude ones too [joke alert]). And I certainly admit I haven't
>written anything up on GenCon either (my excuse being trying so hard to
>stay alive [e.g. Hamblin as a predator and Churchill as a prey in the
>Sabbat draft] that I neglect to remember what I did), but I will
>endeavour to in the future.

Now you see the problem. =) Your focus as a player HAS to be on your
own game, and even when it's not your turn you need to watch and see
how the table politics are happening, who's about to fall, etc.

A local playgroup would be even more difficult (certainly ours, where
the empties get carted out en masse at the end of the night), since
someone would double as a player/reporter. =)

-- Derek
Jack-Booted Thug of Atlanta

Messages.Author: Frederick Scott
Messages.Body:
Joshua Duffin <jt...@cornell.edu> writes:

>Third round, my prey was, umm, forgot his name, playing

>the goal of preventing all your damage and Pulling your
>Fangs, or Disarming you, or both. It looked like a good
>plan, but having twelve minions out is a little too
>obvious, and he was the first to go.

Yep, that is an acknowledged problem with that deck. People see two
or three embraced and a half dozen recruited weenies and absolutely
panic, which I can appreciate. What I didn't know, living on the
west side of the country where it's hard to get to many tournaments,
was how popular Ancilla Empowerments were. I was also kind of surprised
at the pure number of damage votes sprinkled into decks that are not
"vote decks" per se. All through both constructed tournaments I saw
a lot of decks that would start out with stealth/bleed and suddenly
whip out a KRC or Conservative Agitation. Had I understood all this,
I think I had a much better deck in reserve. (Though you can never
tell what vulnerabilities a deck has that you didn't play.) I liked
the fortitude weeny deck because it's much less vulnerable to someone
pulling out an Atonement. But I never saw any Atonements, only those
damn votes.

...

>So after that I bled when I felt like I had a good hand
>of combat cards, and I hoped he would get himself down
>to oust range by buying vampires. He nearly did, too,
>except that he had a couple Wakes in there, and managed
>to oust his prey (Mr. Scott and his horde of weenies)
>with a second damaging vote that the table let him pass
>(the first one was an Ancilla Empowerment that did about
>nine to F. Scott; I didn't think it was a good idea to
>get him killed, but I had no say since I only had about
>one vote if that, and my prey had four and my predator
>about five).

Hard to say. I don't blame him for fearing a table sweep but he did
what a couple other people in other games did that I tried to warn
him against. (It didn't help that my prey was going on and on about how
easy it was to hold out with only a couple blood in your pool. I don't
think he was convincing anyone but I think it may have distracted my
predator from the real danger in the game.) He stopped looking at the
rest of the table and failed to notice the Minion Tap/Fifth Tradition
stuff going on behind you because he was so focused on my hordes and
your combat.

Oh well, live and learn. The lessons of Gencon will probably set me up
perfectly to be just behind the eight ball in tech for whatever large
tournaments I manage to get to next year. At least, that's how it
usually works for me.

Fred

Messages.Author: James Hamblin
Messages.Body:
madma...@my-deja.com wrote:
>
> Hey, doesn't anyone write tournament reports here??

All right, all right.

So I played in the constructed tournament on Thursday. My deck was a
Gangrel intercept deck with lots of untap/intercept/S:CE, lots of pool
gain, a few Claws/Rotschreck, and Smiling Jacks. The deck is basically
impervious to being killed. And, true to form, I never died. I got
half a VP in each of the three rounds I played. I still maintain that I
would have gotten more VP's if the rounds had been a couple hours
longer... :)

Anyway.... I also played in the Sabbat draft on Friday. The face-up
Rochester style was something I had never done before with V:TES. I
played in the booster draft at Origins, but this was definitely more
interesting. About the only downside was the preponderance of
duplicates in the eight cards that we flipped up. About 1/3 of the
time, of the eight cards, there were two pairs.

My plan going into the draft was to make a clan choice, and then stick
to it. I wanted to first-pick a good, medium-sized vampire, and base a
deck around it. I figured that this would at least make my deck
consistent, if not good. Unfortunately, there was a little bump at the
beginning; the first eight vampires' capacities were 2, 3, and 10. I
ended up picking Lambach and his twin brother Lambach (I told you there
were a lot of doubles), thinking I would corner the Vicissitude market.
Then Ian Forestal came up, and I figured I'd corner the
whatever-the-hell-I-wanted market. The !Tremere angle stayed pretty
strong, so that's what I went with. The guy across the table drafted a
bunch of guns, and I drafted six Soul Burns. I got pretty lucky with 3
Bonding, 2 Forced Awakening, 3 Redirection. I ended up with a !Tremere
deck which splashed for Fortitude. I put Lambach in the crypt since he
had votes, aggravated hand damage, and DOM AUS.

The first round, my prey was Madman. I don't recall who the other
players were. My predator was playing !Brujah combat and the
across-the-table guy had a !Gangrel deck. I did a lot of bleeding
early, and everyone else bent over backwards rescuing Madman's vampires
in a vain attempt to keep him alive... at the end, it was Ian Forestal
whipping Fortitude out of his pocket and Daring the Dawn to bleed
Madman's last pool. The rest of the table fell soon after; I was about
2 minutes from bleeding out my predator when time was called.

Having made a pretty good showing, I decided to drop out and do other
cool stuff, like walk around the dealer room. Now, before you berate me
for my lack of commitment, recall that this had been my _fourth_ game in
a row playing up to the time limit. I needed a V:TES break. Besides, I
had to play some Shadowfist... but that's another story.

James
--

Messages.Author: Andrew S. Davidson
Messages.Body:
On Wed, 16 Aug 2000 17:51:39 GMT, madma...@my-deja.com wrote:

>Hey, doesn't anyone write tournament reports here??

I played in one event at Gencon - the Sabbat draft. I had supposed
that this would be the same format that I saw at Origins - open the
booster, take a card, pass it on. Instead it was a Rochester draft -
open the booster but don't look, put two cards in the middle and then
draft from this common pool until all gone and then repeat. I like
the other drafting method but this format was awful. Folk who were
not intimately familiar with Sabbat (most of us) needed to look at the
cards closely and this was only possible when it was your turn to pick
a card. On our table, we put the cards on the back of a play-mat and
passed it around. This procedure took forever because most of the
time was dead-time - waiting for your turn to come round. You weren't
even allowed to look at existing cards between picks.

The drafting process took about 2 hours. I built a combat deck that
didn't come out too well and I was ousted first on my table. I then
happily escaped from this torture and entered the Shadowfist Can o'
Whupass event. This was sealed deck - one starter and 3 boosters. I
built a good hi-tech deck in about 10 minutes and then started kicking
butt. That's more like it.

The Sabbat event was sold out and so some keen players had to play
pick-up instead. Why turn people away? I'd have thought another
table of 5 could have been added without trouble. Anyway, I'm never
going to try this format again and so that's one place freed up.

Andrew

Messages.Author: Frederick Scott
Messages.Body:
a...@csi.com (Andrew S. Davidson) writes:

>I played in one event at Gencon - the Sabbat draft. I had supposed
>that this would be the same format that I saw at Origins - open the
>booster, take a card, pass it on. Instead it was a Rochester draft -

>passed it around. This procedure took forever because most of the
>time was dead-time - waiting for your turn to come round. You weren't
>even allowed to look at existing cards between picks.

Yea, that was a bad way to do it. You should have objected. Our table
just left the cards in the center and gave the person currently drafting
the priority if he wanted to turn all the cards in his direction. Usually,
it wasn't necessary, so you could read any cards you needed to read while
others were drafting. (The main problem was that most of the cards that
needed reading, everybody needed to read them.)

The problem I had with it was that you had so little control over what
came up and when that a lot of it was almost as badly luck as sealed
deck. You start concentrating on presense and a killer presense bleed
cards comes up when you were drafting fifth so you're just screwed. I
kept getting lousy choices when I drafted first and then first pick would
rotate around to my left and the guy would get something absolutely
sensational. Well, all right, I'm whining now and my problems in this
tournament were a lot more self-inflicted than luck-inflicted but you
get the point. Luck does play a major role in table draft - much more
so, IMHO, than booster draft.

>The Sabbat event was sold out and so some keen players had to play
>pick-up instead. Why turn people away?

Let's see, you can get 5 booster packs of Sabbat, current market price
in the $40-50 range (that's right folks!!!), for $12 and you're wondering
why they had a limit on players? Easy: 1) there's a limit to their
largesse; and 2) with no limit, it would be hard to predict how many
people you'd have to arrange to have Sabbat packs for. Did you think
they just have boxes and boxes of the things stacked up in some White
Wolf warehouse somewhere?

Fred

Yea, that was a bad way to do it. You should have objected. Our table

just left the cards in the center and gave the person currently drafting
the priority if he wanted to turn all the cards in his direction. Usually,

sensational. Well, all right, I'm whining now and my problems in this
tournament were a lot more self-inflicted than luck-inflicted but you
get the point. Luck does play a major role in table draft - much more
so, IMHO, than booster draft.

>>Yep, that is an acknowledged problem with that deck. People see two
>>or three embraced and a half dozen recruited weenies and absolutely
>>panic, which I can appreciate.

>not so amazed anymore) that the rest of the table will jump on anyone
>who has a lot of ready minions. Me? I think it's silly. 5th/Tap
>decks are, IMHO, much more dangerous over the long run.

Whew. Perhaps in the long run, but if you have intercept, that 5th
isn't going to get off and that vampire is going to be dead. Simply
put, more actions is ALWAYS better, and a guy with eight minions HAS
to be made dead, or he is extremely likely to sweep. The guy with two
minions doing MT/5th is a threat, yeah, but you have a good chance of
ousting a prey or two on your own before the MT/5 deck gets up and
running. The guy with 8 minions is likely to get you at any point in
time.

>Any advice (other than "Don't play weenies") would be appreciated.

Bad news. "Don't play weenies" is the only -useful- advice.

Weenies are strong. They take lots of actions for little cost. But
they generally go "pop!" in combat, they tend to have problems with
votes (no inherent titles and vulnerable to Domain Challenge/Ancilla
Empowerment), and they're a BIG-ass target. Short of a generous
supply of Delaying Tactics or a hideous Weenie Vote Deck, I don't see
a way to keep yourself from getting mugged by people dropping one or
two Ancillas in their deck as weenie defense. your advantage, though,
is that not many people include Ancillas as weenie defense - except in
tournaments. =)

As Derek said, 5th/Tap decks can be very strong (and
annoyingly hard to kill) in a long game - if they live
that long. Which usually means, if they don't get their
5ths blocked. Or get their vamps rushed and killed.
Early on, it can be a delicate deck because you only
have one or two vamps to work with.

[frederick scott, then madman]

> >What I didn't know, living on the west side of the country
> >where it's hard to get to many tournaments,
> >was how popular Ancilla Empowerments were.
>
> Or try Domain Challenge, etc. Of course, my weenies rarely have much
> in the way of votes so I'm a sitting duck for that sorta stuff <sigh>.
>
> Any advice (other than "Don't play weenies") would be appreciated.

As Derek mentioned, Delaying Tactics is really quite
good for vote defense, especially if you're playing
a fast deck where you'll only need to be defended for
a few turns before you get an oust. You can Wake and
Delay if you need to act with all your minions, too.
For combat defense with weenies, I like disciplineless
Dodge (combined with Fake Outs if you're really paranoid).
If they're not trying too hard, they may not be able to
get past it, and if they are a serious combat deck,
they have to use their serious combat cards every time
to beat your Dodge, and you may get to save some of your
poor weak vampires that way.

For bleed defense, well, I guess weenies don't really
have any. Archon Investigation (oh how cruel) for the
big bleeds; for the smaller ones you're pretty much
stuck with racing (ie oust your prey before your predator
ousts you).

Josh

It's an issue of waste. Did you have the right to play? Yes. Did you get
there first, buy the ticket, and show up? Yes. However it was a waste of a
slot in the _tournament_. What is the point playing in a tournament when you
have no intention of playing the entire tournament? You could have played in
the pick up game and had a good time playing. The point of the tournament is
to compete in a organized event against other players and determine a final
winner. It's not to play one game, have a good time, decide your tired of
VTES, and then leave. You knew the time and demands involved in playing in a
VTES tournament. Why did you bother to start if you where already getting
tired of the game?

It's like a guy walking up to the snack bar and jumping in front of someone
else who is starving. He buys the last sandwich takes two bites and throws
the rest in the garbage disposal. Did he have the right to do so? Yes. Did
he enjoy his two bites? Yes. However it's a terrible waste that really
screws the guy who is starving. Does the starving guy have a right to be
pissed? I think so.

In short, yes I do think you should have sold the slot to someone waiting in
line. If the tournament is really so unimportant, enough so you would drop
out after the first round, why take up the slot.

Steve Bucy

Messages.Body:

> To the final end, I sort of wish they'd changed at least one of those two
> duel tournaments to a constructed of some sort, preferable (IMO) just
> vanilla rules like on Thursday.

Not possible, due to the time constraints: single elim duel tourneys require
a time commitment of 2.5 hours. Multi-player tournaments require at
least a seven hour time commitment (for a abbreviated 2+F situation).

> I would like to have seen at least three
> VEKN rules constructed over the four days, myself. And duels are a pretty
> specialized form of play to have two events dedicated to them.

The two events weren't "dedicated" to them - the duels were simply put into
the schedule to fill holes that couldn't be filled by regular tournaments
(at least by my schedule). One (the Friday night duel) was even scheduled to
begin at the same time as the Sabbat Draft finals in order to maximize the
opportunities players would have to play.

Without the duels, those "events" would simply have been non-events.
The duels didn't replace any other events.

Anyone desiring more VEKN constructed events (at major conventions or not) is
free to make that happen. See the web page for information on sanctioning
tournaments through the VEKN.

On Thu, 17 Aug 2000 07:51:23 -0400, LSJ wrote:

>The "boxes and boxes" you've seen have all been handed out at Dragon*Con,
>Origins, and Gen*Con - Gen*Con represented the end of those "boxes and
>boxes".

I see. It's academic now but you could have stretched the available
supplies by forgoing the 5th booster in the third round and using
these to fill up another table or two. I wouldn't have minded.

The format might be improved if there was less up-front drafting and
additional drafting between each round. I've done something similar
with Shadowfist events - just giving each player a starter at the
outset and then table drafting a booster after each round, starting
with the winner. This provides a good incentive to win each game and
breaks up the drafting into less wearisome interludes. If we'd only
drafted 2 Sabbat boosters each at the outset, say, then the initial
drafting time would have been halved (~1 hour instead of 2) and the
first round might have been over more quickly as the starting decks
would be tend to be smaller. There would then have been time and
incentive to stick around for a second round of drafting rather than
exiting after an early 1st-round ousting.

There was a Michigan draft event too. How did that work?

Andrew

they can. That is just the way it works sometimes. VTES tournaments

Norman wrote:

tourney for no other reason than to go play a game of Shadowfist. I was
at work on a Saturday when I wrote the former posts and was nessasarily

(From here on in, I'm talking completely hypothetically about the subject at
hand, and not really talking issue with what Norman wrote in any way).

I fully understand how someone would be bothered by someone else dropping out
of a tournament--I have been in tournaments where people dropped out half way
through, and it was a pain (heck, we waited around for an hour once 'cause our
10th guy said "I'm going to get lunch, I'll be right back..." and then decided
to go home after he ate lunch, telling no one), but it happens, and there
really isn't anything to do about it.

I certainly agree that "strip mining" (is that an actual term, or did someone
just make it up here? Either way, it cracks me up :-), entering a sealed/draft
tournament just to get the cards with no intention of actually playing, is an
etically questionable action. If I had my dithers, this would be simply
verboten, but how do you really enforce such an idea?

Clearly there are situations where dropping out of a tournament is
justified--you fall ill; your mom comes to pick you up; you have to get up
early for work and the tournament is taking forever; you gotta go pick up your
wife. Clearly "strip mining" is something that pretty much everyone would like
to do away with. What about the grey areas? What if someone shows up to a
tournament after not having played for a long time, has a very questionable
deck, and gets horribly killed in the first round, and they don't think that is
worth their effort continuing? What if someone goes to a 4 round tournament
with an "experimental" deck, and after getting totally trashed in the first 2
rounds, they have the choice of either getting certainly trashed in the 3rd
round *or* dropping out to go play a different game that, if they stick around
to get trashed, they will not get to play? At what point does it become
acceptable to drop out and at what point is it just irresponsible to drop out?

The answer is that there is no answer--this is simply something that can't
really be controlled, as one person's completely legitimate reason to leave ("I
feel like crap and I need some sleep, other wise I'll be *really* cranky for
the rest of the tournament and I'll just piss everyone off.") is another
person's lame excuse to screw up the tournament. As long as adaquate notice is
given, I can't see any situation where I would feel justified getting upset at
someone for dropping out.

next league, we are going to inform him that either he shows up and
stays for the game, or he shouldn't join. If he does it even once, he
will be kicked out of the league. It's TERRIBLY poor sportsmanship.
Everyone playing in the league agrees heartily with the decision, too.

Now, I understand that sometimes things happen which are unavoidable
and require withdrawal, and it's the tournament organizer's job to
deal with this. But just leaving because you're losing, or because
you wanted to strip-mine the tourney, rises to one of the few, proud
pinnacles of lameness.

>I remember travelling a long distance in a stuffy car with 5 Magic
>players to make it to my very first Regional tournament. I didn't get
>to play because the tournament was overbooked. It sucked, and yes, I
>resented the players that dropped after a few rounds. But my resentment
>didn't make their dropping a _wrong_ thing.

No, the fact that they dropped is a wrong thing in itself, no matter
if anyone was pissed or not.

>If someone does drop for the cards, that's the way it is.

And it's still lame as hell, unethical, and childish.

>If they drop because they are a minor, and their parents say they have
>to go, that's the way it is.

THIS is an unavoidable situation for the PLAYER, and shouldn't be held
against him. Unless, of course, he knew he'd have to leave and
wouldn't be able to finish and signed up anyway.

>In Magic tournaments, people rare-draft ALL the time and drop as soon as
>they can. That is just the way it works sometimes. VTES tournaments

That's because a lot of Magic players are some of the biggest and most
fucking pathetic losers I've ever seen in my life. Pardon my
language, but I do NOT think that we want V:TES to become at ALL like
Magic, ESPECIALLY as regards to the type of people we have playing!

There are always going to be losers in the world. Let's encourage
them to stop being losers and act like real people, instead of
continuing to be losers. Some of them will actually change if they
find that being lame is not tolerated. Some of them will not; shit
happens. But just turning a blind eye to things is not going to
improve the CCG community, nor is it going to improve the public view
of the CCG community, which is currently VERY skewed. In case you
think it doesn't matter what the public thinks, you're wrong - the
public is where our new players will come from. We had damned well
better look good, or if we can't do that, we had better not look BAD.

>may be rarer, but that doesn't change that some people can choose to be
>in a draft for the cards, and not for the tourney. That the way it is.

This is why I advocate not holding draft tournaments for rare cards.
Since there is no effective way to keep people from strip-mining a
tourney (chaining them to the tables is impolite), why encourage
lameness? It's simply a bad idea.



Messages.Author: Derek Ray
Messages.Body:
On Fri, 18 Aug 2000 18:43:48 +0000, James Hamblin
<ham...@math.wisc.edu> wrote:

>Derek Ray wrote:
>> The repeat dropout performances have personally convinced me that we
>> shouldn't do draft tournaments with any cards that are actually in
>> demand.
>
>Having draft tournaments with cards that are in demand is what gets
>people to play in those tournaments.

Obviously not, since a number of people didn't bother to play, and
strip-mining tourneys is apparently very common in Magic. It gets
people to sign up for the tourneys, sure, but it doesn't necessarily
get 'em to play.

Also, if a constructed-deck event had been held in the same time slot,
there still would have been a lot of players. Nope, doesn't wash.

(Oh, I consider 25 players in a Jyhad draft tournament pretty damn
good, too. The vast majority of Jyhad cards are DEFINITELY not in
demand. Funny, that.)

>example; there are draft tournaments with hard-to-get card sets which
>attract a lot of people for that reason. Some people go into those

>tournaments to grab some cards and run. Why is that a problem?

Because it's unethical, lame, and really trashes the image of the game
in people's eyes. "Geez, they don't even play the game... they just

CCGs being a crack habit.

I do not usually volunteer the information that I play/collect a CCG
to non-gamers, because CCGs still have a very bad reputation in the
non-gaming world (and even parts of the gaming world). We need to be

>And, once again: that is not what I did. I played in the tournament and
>decided to drop after one round. I did not go into the tournament
>intending to drop after the first round. But even if I had, there
>shouldn't be a problem with that.

You will, of course, notice that I carefully accused nobody by name,
and specifically stated that I was NOT accusing anyone of actually
doing that.

There shouldn't be a problem with that? Have you no sense of
sportsmanship at all? This strikes me as a very selfish statement -
assuming that your time is significantly more valuable than anyone
else's. You made a commitment by entering the tournament, to play in
3 rounds and potentially a final. There are no direct penalties for
breaking that commitment, but you STILL made one and should have the
class to honor it.

>You make it sound like I'm some sort of horrible person for managing to
>get my event ticket before you, and then (in your opinion) misusing it.

And in the opinion of a damned lot of other people, too. However,
again keep in mind that I did not attend at all, and so I am not one
of the "screwed" people. These are not merely "sour grapes"
arguments.

>I really resent this implication. If it had been a Jyhad draft, I would

>have dropped out at the same time for the same reason.
>

>But AGAIN: even if I hadn't, I would still have felt completely
>justified.

This also strikes me as an extremely selfish statement.

I have other comments, but they can be found in my post to the
Corrupter, and I see no need to repeat them unnecessarily - but the
one about the pool league we're running is the most relevant.

It's impossible for me to grasp because it's completely unreasonable.

> If it were the intent of the organizers to sell Sabbat boosters at 4

As is the case with most draft tournaments in my experience, you had to

> We are currently dealing with a similar situation in a pool league

It's WRONG? Huh? I really don't understand...

> >If someone does drop for the cards, that's the way it is.
>
> And it's still lame as hell, unethical, and childish.

I'd rather have people getting the cards any way they can. To White
Wolf, the success or failure of V:TES will be based on sales. It will

And: UNETHICAL? Huh?

[Snip: Magic players are generally losers, and society thinks CCGers are
weirdos]

OK, just because you think you play a superior game doesn't mean you
have some sort of superior morality. Some of most cultured and
intelligent people I know (including one Adrian Sullivan) play Magic.
Your generalization is as false and unfair as the one a random person
would make about card games as a whole. You may think your silly
vampire card game is better than the other silly card games, but to the
general public, they're all silly card games.

> >may be rarer, but that doesn't change that some people can choose to be
> >in a draft for the cards, and not for the tourney. That the way it is.
>
> This is why I advocate not holding draft tournaments for rare cards.
> Since there is no effective way to keep people from strip-mining a
> tourney (chaining them to the tables is impolite), why encourage
> lameness? It's simply a bad idea.

"This is why I advocate not letting people play stealth and bleed
decks. Since there's no effective way to keep people from playing those
kinds of decks (ripping up their Malkavians is impolite), why encourage
lameness?"

You may not like that people choose to exercise their free will and do
things that you don't agree with. But get off your high horse and
accept that people are going to do whatever the hell they want to. It
is reasonable to expect someone to finish a game. It is reasonable to

Messages.Author: Andrew S. Davidson
Messages.Body:
On Sat, 19 Aug 2000 15:39:43 GMT, X_Ze...@email.msn.com wrote:

>Are you actually advocating strip-mining a tournament? There is no
>reason to ever join a tournament only to quit half-way through, whether
>it is a Sabbat tournament or a golf tournament. If you are going to

>play then play, not play and then quit. It spoils the victory of

>winning a tournament if half the competion quit for whatever reason.

Quitting can be perfectly sportsmanlike, e.g. resigning a chess game
or declaring in cricket. The trouble with the Vampite events is that
the 3 round format takes lots of time, especially if there's a 2 hour
drafting session up front. At a big convention, it's unreasonable to
expect players to press on regardless if they see that their cause is
hopeless and there are other events opening up. It's probably better
for all concerned if no-hope players drop out. Force them to stay in
when they don't want to and you risk creating a loose cannon - they'll
start doing things for the hell of it, just to have some fun.

Andrew

Messages.Author: Frederick Scott
Messages.Body:
X_Ze...@email.msn.com writes (about why resigning in a V:tES tournament
is unethical):

>Certainly it is alright to resign in a game of Jyhad once it has become
>hopeless, but you do not quit out of a double elimination chess or
>cricket tournament (may I remind you that VTES tourneys are
>considered to be triple elimination). The reason for this is because
>how you play influences who gets to the finals. It is extremely unfair
>to play the first round (especially if you are playing a intercept deck
>or a anarch revolt deck) and deprive someone of victory points, then
>drop out and not deny victory points to the opponents that should be
>playing you later in the tournament. I would agree with you if VTES
>tourneys were single elimination, but as they are not, I do not.

I'm not sure you have this analyzed very well. You do not "not deny
victory points" to your later opponents. The tables just get reshuffled
and they get a different game than they would have gotten otherwise.
It's not like each round is fixed and if a person drops out of the
tournament, those who would play against his position get an empty seat
and a free victory point.

As an aside, that would be weird - show up at a 5-person table, find
two people have dropped so you're playing a three-person game. I'd be
mad about having to play the three-person game, never mind the potential
for two free victory points. And I suppose the predators of the "empty
chairs" would also get 6 free pool as well as their free VP as they
started off? (What about the third guy? Or both the other guys if one
player got both empty seats as prey. Yuck!)

But this isn't what happens, of course. So ethics based on such assumptions
are not valid in real V:tES tournaments. In reality, the quitters leave
and take their table positions and victory points and six pool reward for
ousting with them. If they don't tell the judge before they go, he has
the headache of trying to move things around just before the next round
starts (so leaving without warning is a distinct trangression), but the
remaining players should be as challenged by the competition as those who
played against the quitter in earlier rounds.

In fact, if you assume the quitters had reason to leave and that
reason was they their deck sucked (or their play or both) then future
opponents actually get screwed by losing the opportunity to play them
after the quitters' first round opponents got such a chance. That kind
of speculation gets pretty conjectural though, so is not worth engaging
in.

Fred

Messages.Body:
On Mon, 21 Aug 2000 00:04:26 -0500, James Hamblin
<ham...@math.wisc.edu> wrote:

>Well, I had a well-crafted, thoughtful response ready to go, and then my
>computer crashed. Oh, well.

I damned near deleted an entire page of my own by accidentally
dropping my mouse on the corner of the keyboard- which included the
"page up" and "delete" keys.

>Derek Ray wrote:
>>
>> On Fri, 18 Aug 2000 19:55:03 GMT, thecor...@yahoo.com wrote:
>>
>> >But it doesn't make it an individual players responsibility not to drop.
>>
>> Individual players entering a tournament should at least intend to
>> play the tournament. How difficult is this to grasp for some of you?
>
>It's impossible for me to grasp because it's completely unreasonable.
>You can't force people to attend the entirety of a 7-10 hour event. You
>have to understand that people are going to want to leave, and you can't
>stop them.

I totally, completely, and utterly fail to see how this is
unreasonable. You warn players ahead of time "This tournament will
require a 7-10 hour commitment." They then can make a nice, reasoned
decision with some forethought as to whether they wish to burn 7-10
hours of their time. If they do not wish to, THEY SHOULD NOT ENTER.
Why is asking people to have a clue so terribly unreasonable?

And you are correct, we cannot stop them. We can attempt to
discourage them from doing so, and the only way is to explain to them
why it is rude to just bail in the middle because they're losing, or
to just bail in the middle to grab the cards and run.

>> If it were the intent of the organizers to sell Sabbat boosters at 4
>> for $10, they would just have bloody well set it up to be a booster
>> sale, first come first served.
>
>As is the case with most draft tournaments in my experience, you had to
>play in the first round of the tournament in order to keep the cards.
>So in that sense, participation was mandatory. It wasn't a cheap-o
>booster sale.

How will you stop someone from standing up from the initial table, or
FINDING a way to stand up, and just vanishing? The rule about "you
must play in the first round" is just as un-enforceable as a rule
about "you must play in all the third round". Currently several
people have noted a problem with the Rochester draft: that playing on
the same table that you drafted on tends to make people excessively
counterdraft as opposed to drafting for their own improvement. If you
sit everyone down and then re-seat the tables after the draft, you
provide a sufficient moment of run-in-circles confusion that players
who don't wish to play in the first round can leave, and nobody will
notice 'til too late. And really, what will you do if you DO notice -
run after them shouting "hey! where are you going with those cards
you paid for?"

>Clearly, he shouldn't leave in the middle of the game. That's just
>rude. But why can't he leave between games? He says "thanks, nice
>game, gotta go" and leaves. Why is that so reprehensible? Why force
>him to stay and do something he doesn't want to do?

Your next paragraph defines it quite well in the second sentence, but
I can state it clearly this way as well. Assume the league match is a
race to 11, which means "the first person to win 11 games wins." I am
playing Fats. I get up 4-0 on Fats early on with some wild, wack-ass
lucky shotmaking. Fats, inbetween games, says 'Gotta go' and leaves.

Fats has got pissed and quit when he had a PERFECTLY reasonable chance
of winning. From your definition: it wasn't fair to me, since I got
screwed out of playing time I'd have enjoyed. It wasn't respectful to
me, since I really have done nothing at 4-0 to deserve respect. It is
DEFINITELY not graciousness in losing, since graciousness in losing
would involve sticking around and making an effort to win. I don't
enter tournaments to see people roll over when they find my name
matched up against theirs in the brackets - I enter to see if I can
still win, knowing that people are gunning for me.

Avoiding the "respect" one, which might be vague, I get 2 out of 3
definite qualifications for 'unsportsmanlike' from that, and a third
out of 3 that would be quite debatable on both sides.

>I looked up "sportsmanship" in the dictionary, since to me, it's quite a
>vague term. I got "fairness, respect for one's opponent, and
>graciousness in winning or losing." How is entering a tournament and
>quitting between rounds unsportsmanlike? It's not unfair to the TO;
>they know how to deal with it. It's not unfair to the other players;
>you finished the games you were in. Maybe in your opinion it's
>ingracious; but what if I'm not quitting because I'm losing?

It's unfair to the other players because it affects the future rounds.

If you have a deck that is completely pants, it has gained no VPs
itself, but it probably has rolled over very nicely for its initial
predator, unbalancing the table -against- 3 other players. Luck of
the draw, but all V:TES players understand that sort of thing.
However, if you remove a weak deck from play, it makes it that much
harder for ANYONE else to gain VPs, no matter who gets lucky and draws
it as initial-prey. That first predator gains an unfair advantage
through your withdrawal, whereas three predators should have.

If you have a deck that isn't pants but just isn't any fun (an Anarch
Revolt/Smiling Jack deck that really hosed up your first table and
scattered VPs everywhere), it's still unfair, since you should sit
down at two other tables and screw THOSE up as well. Now you've made
VPs easier to get for everyone EXCEPT your initial 4 opponents.

If you have a deck that is GOOD but isn't any fun, (weenie dominate
bleed), that's most unfair of all since you, perhaps, gain 4 VPs from
your first table, get bored with weenie dominate, and leave. You have
made VPs MUCH easier to get for everyone except your first 4
opponents.

It's not respectful, because you assume that your time is more
important than everyone else's time, and so it's OK for you to screw
up the mechanics and complicate things. This really is quite
disrespectful of all the other players who were willing to commit the
full 8 hours.

If you bail because your deck sucks, it isn't graciousness in losing
at all, obviously. If you bail because your deck is winning and is
boring, it's absolutely not graciousness in winning - it's like
dumping out in the final brackets of a pool tourney and saying "Naw,
you guys are too easy. 4th is fine for me, i'll let someone else win
this one."

It's not too difficult to go through and discover why bailing out is
unsportsmanlike. If you didn't realize the tournament would last that
long when you signed up, that's one thing (although you should learn
to read, since the time-block is set out that way), but if you
knowingly sign up for a 7-10 hour commitment, you really ought to
remain.

>This sort of reminds me of the card limit debate. A card limit player
>might say "We don't like when people play stealth and bleed. Those
>people are bad people." You're saying "I don't like it when people
>enter a tournament and then drop. Those people (i.e., people like me)
>are bad people."

False analogy. Stealth and bleed is disliked because it is an
effective way to accomplish the purpose of the game: to gain the most
VPs and thereby win. Dropping from a tournament does NOT accomplish
the stated purpose of entering the tournament: to gain VPs, get to the
finals, and win.

>> No, the fact that they dropped is a wrong thing in itself, no matter
>> if anyone was pissed or not.
>
>It's WRONG? Huh? I really don't understand...

Respect for one's fellow opponents. Enough respect to remain and
finish. To actually play the game instead of grab the cards and run.
To give it your best shot in a poor situation (you could get lucky and
sit in front of ANOTHER crap deck, or sit as the predator of the one
deck who couldn't deal with you). I've swept tables with my Tremere
weenie Rush-n-burn deck. I've garnered 0 VPs with it far more often
than I've swept, but occasionally you get a prey who just can't handle
THA combat, and you get off to a flashing start.

>I'd rather have people getting the cards any way they can. To White
>Wolf, the success or failure of V:TES will be based on sales. It will
>not be based on whether the people making those purchases are considered
>lame by one Derek Ray.

The success or failure of V:TES will be based on sales in the retail
outlets, NOT by booster draft tournaments for out-of-print sets.
White Wolf would be MAD to use the number of entries into a booster
draft as anything other than the most fringe indicator of how popular
the game is. If the sales in the retail outlets are sufficient, the
game will be considered to be doing well, because the retail outlets
will order more boxes in large quantities. Much larger than for a
solitary booster tourney.

>OK, just because you think you play a superior game doesn't mean you
>have some sort of superior morality. Some of most cultured and
>intelligent people I know (including one Adrian Sullivan) play Magic.

Congratulations. I went out of my way to use words that permitted
individual exceptions for certain Magic players, and sure enough,
someone jumped in and said "but _____ is a nice guy, you rotter!"

That's great. I knew there would be plenty of actual decent human
beings that play Magic as well. In fact, some of our group used to
play. But you know what? There really are a whole boatload of
fucking losers playing Magic, as WELL as the decent, cultured,
intelligent people. Why? I don't know. Just because you dislike the
fact, and dislike that it gets brought up a lot, doesn't make it any
less true, OR any less relevant.

Right now V:TES doesn't have anywhere near the loser-to-human ratio
that some other games do. I haven't met very many people from V:TES
that I just cringe at the thought of encountering again, and I can't
even think of one off the top of my head. I want to see V:TES become
hugely popular. With that popularity will come losers to play the
game, possibly LOTS, and I accept that as just life. But that doesn't
mean we need to encourage them to continue being losers while playing
with us, and we have a great opportunity while the community is still
fairly small. I don't really know any other way to state it, and if
you still don't understand what I'm saying, I can't help you.

My purpose was not to say "V:TES is better than Magic, nyah nyah" - it
was to show where we could end up if we're not careful. Showing
tolerance of "strip-mining" tournaments for rare cards horrifies me.
While it may not be possible to prevent, it can definitely be actively
discouraged, which will help lots.

>Your generalization is as false and unfair as the one a random person
>would make about card games as a whole. You may think your silly
>vampire card game is better than the other silly card games, but to the
>general public, they're all silly card games.

And as such, the general public will form its opinions of the card
game based on the most well-known one: Magic. And that's not serving
as an especially good front-man right now, other than to show how CCGs
can make shedloads of money off of gamers.

[snip repeat of false analogy about strip mining = stealth bleed]

>You may not like that people choose to exercise their free will and do
>things that you don't agree with. But get off your high horse and
>accept that people are going to do whatever the hell they want to. It

OK. I accept that some people are going to be selfish buggers and
break commitments at their whim. This doesn't mean that I have to
tolerate it, and it doesn't mean that I won't speak out against it
whenever I see fit, and it doesn't mean that I won't attempt to come
up with ideas that prevent people from being selfish buggers at the
expense of others.

>is reasonable to expect someone to finish a game. It is reasonable to
>expect someone to play _some_ part of a tournament that they enter. But
>just because you think people should stay for the whole thing doesn't
>mean you can make them do it, and it doesn't mean they should do it,
>either.

It doesn't mean that I can make them do it. But i'm afraid that
committing to play in a 7-10 hour tournament -does- mean that one
SHOULD stay for the full thing.

>[If I get personally attacked again, this will be the last I say on the
>subject. Note: "Your argument is unreasonable" is not a personal
>attack. "You are a terrible person of low character" _is_ a personal
>attack.]

Fine. Please identify where I said you were a terrible person of low
character?

[my own aside]

This whole set of posts may sound a bit forward from me, especially
when I wasn't involved originally. But I dealt with running
double-elimination pool tournaments on a regular basis for several
years, with significant money involved for winning, and significant
money on the side in a player auction/Calcutta. It required
absolutely no effort on my part to deal with a drop, since
double-elimination brackets are very easy - I just scratch that
person's name out and write in "BYE", and anyone who has to play that
person automatically wins and advances.

However, it generally drew some pretty snarly disfavor and commentary
from everyone else involved in the tourney. Partly because someone
was usually getting a bit of a free ride by the dropout, instead of
having to play a match they might well not have won. Partly because
the person who bought them in the player auction just got COMPLETELY
screwed. But it was more interesting to hear the complaints be echoed
by the person who benefitted from the drop! They'd say "Well, hey,
i'll take it, but he could've at least PLAYED and lost." In my
experience over 3 years, I never once encountered the attitude that it
was "ok" for someone to just dump out in the middle on a whim, nor did
I ever treat it as 'ok' when they came to me and said "I'm pissed, i'm
leaving." Sometimes nobody was especially pissed about it, but the
collective attitude did come down to "it's just unsportsmanlike. If
you want to get out that badly, just lose on purpose." Which is also
unsportsmanlike, but much less so than "BYE" in big letters in the
fourth round winners' side.

Messages.Author: James Hamblin
Messages.Body:
Derek Ray wrote:
>
> On Mon, 21 Aug 2000 00:04:26 -0500, James Hamblin
> <ham...@math.wisc.edu> wrote:
>
> >Well, I had a well-crafted, thoughtful response ready to go, and then my
> >computer crashed. Oh, well.
>
> I damned near deleted an entire page of my own by accidentally
> dropping my mouse on the corner of the keyboard- which included the
> "page up" and "delete" keys.

Ah, the dangers of newsgroup posting... :)

> >Derek Ray wrote:
> >>
> >> Individual players entering a tournament should at least intend to
> >> play the tournament. How difficult is this to grasp for some of you?
> >
> >It's impossible for me to grasp because it's completely unreasonable.
> >You can't force people to attend the entirety of a 7-10 hour event. You
> >have to understand that people are going to want to leave, and you can't
> >stop them.
>
> I totally, completely, and utterly fail to see how this is
> unreasonable. You warn players ahead of time "This tournament will
> require a 7-10 hour commitment." They then can make a nice, reasoned
> decision with some forethought as to whether they wish to burn 7-10
> hours of their time. If they do not wish to, THEY SHOULD NOT ENTER.
> Why is asking people to have a clue so terribly unreasonable?

_If_ the event said "you will have to stay for the whole event" (which
IIRC some listings did say at GenCon), then your point would be valid.
So one solution to the problem you perceive would be to insert this
clause in the description of each V:TES event ever. But I think
attendence would drop. I for one would be less likely to enter such an
event if I had the slightest suspicion that I might want to bail
part-way through. I get the impression that you would be glad not to
have me. :P

But is it really desirable to do this? Talking about the impression
this would give to the general community: "Oh, that looks like a fun
game, but I don't know if I'd want to play it for 10 hours." The length
of the game is already a deterrent for new players. If you're going to
say "well, then those people shouldn't play in a tournament" I would
respond with: what about players (like, until recently, me) who don't
have a group to play with, and whose _only_ opportunity to play this
game is at conventions? This proposal might shut some of them out.

> And you are correct, we cannot stop them. We can attempt to
> discourage them from doing so, and the only way is to explain to them
> why it is rude to just bail in the middle because they're losing, or
> to just bail in the middle to grab the cards and run.

Or to bail in the middle because they're tired and want to do something
else? You seem to forget that that's the reason I left. It had nothing
to do with losing (I had just won). The fact that I took some cards
with me when I left wasn't the _reason_ I left, it was a side-effect of
the fact that it was a limited-format event.

But, enough about me. What about those people that show up and drop out
because they're losing? I still don't see why it's so terrible for them
to drop out between rounds. I think you overestimate the effect it has
on the rest of the tournament at large. If it were a small event, I can
understand pressuring someone to stay to maintain the "integrity" of the
event.

Note: I've been playing card games in tournaments for years, and this is
the very first time I've been given a hard time for dropping before the
end of the tournament.

> >As is the case with most draft tournaments in my experience, you had to
> >play in the first round of the tournament in order to keep the cards.
> >So in that sense, participation was mandatory. It wasn't a cheap-o
> >booster sale.
>
> How will you stop someone from standing up from the initial table, or
> FINDING a way to stand up, and just vanishing?

That's a completely different issue. In a more organized game, like
Magic, there are ways to discipline players for doing such things.

> Your next paragraph defines it quite well in the second sentence, but
> I can state it clearly this way as well. Assume the league match is a
> race to 11, which means "the first person to win 11 games wins." I am
> playing Fats. I get up 4-0 on Fats early on with some wild, wack-ass
> lucky shotmaking. Fats, inbetween games, says 'Gotta go' and leaves.

OK, I think I understand this better now. I agree: your friend should
be aware that a match is 11 games, and should stay for the whole thing.
Let's say (for some reason) the matches were best of 5. Would you
accept someone completing their match, then leaving?

[snip]

I clipped this argument, but let me try to summarize: whatever kind of
deck you have, it has a specific kind of effect on the table you play
at. By dropping out, you are removing that effect from future tables.
But I argue that the table will get filled up by someone else (after the
seating gets arranged without the drop-out) and their deck will have
some (possibly different) effect on the table. But this is completely
unpredictable. And, again, I think you overestimate the effect this has
on the tournament.

> It's not respectful, because you assume that your time is more
> important than everyone else's time, and so it's OK for you to screw
> up the mechanics and complicate things. This really is quite
> disrespectful of all the other players who were willing to commit the
> full 8 hours.

Nothing becomes complicated: the TO just seats the round without me.
The only way it would be complicated is if the drop wasn't notified
until after the round was seated, and then it would have to be
re-seated. I have never gone into a tournament saying to myself: no
matter what, I am going to stay the whole time. If I have something
better to do, and I'm not leaving in the middle of the game, I'm going
to leave. I will notify the proper authority and, if appropriate,
apologize for any inconvenience, but I will leave if I want to.

> If you bail because your deck sucks, it isn't graciousness in losing
> at all, obviously.

I still don't see how this is ingracious. I lose, I shake my opponent's
hand, say "nice game", and leave.

> It's not too difficult to go through and discover why bailing out is
> unsportsmanlike. If you didn't realize the tournament would last that
> long when you signed up, that's one thing (although you should learn
> to read, since the time-block is set out that way), but if you
> knowingly sign up for a 7-10 hour commitment, you really ought to
> remain.

Why? I didn't sign up for a 7-10 hour commitment. I signed up for an
event that I knew would last 7-10 hours _if_ I stayed to the end. I
decided not to stay until the end. _Especially_ at a convention, where
7-10 hours is a significant percentage of the entire weekend (about
15-20% of the time I spent there the whole weekend), why should I waste
my time?

> False analogy. Stealth and bleed is disliked because it is an
> effective way to accomplish the purpose of the game: to gain the most
> VPs and thereby win. Dropping from a tournament does NOT accomplish
> the stated purpose of entering the tournament: to gain VPs, get to the
> finals, and win.

My purpose in playing in the tournament was to have a good time. I
accomplished that purpose both days I played V:TES, even though I gained
minimal VP's and never made it to the finals. And what if you are at
the point where it is impossible for you to accomplish the goals you
state? Why not drop out then?

> >> No, the fact that they dropped is a wrong thing in itself, no matter
> >> if anyone was pissed or not.
> >
> >It's WRONG? Huh? I really don't understand...
>
> Respect for one's fellow opponents.

Your opponents don't care if there's one less person hanging around or
not.

> Enough respect to remain and
> finish.

Respect for who? If I'm playing my VIC/PRO all aggravated damage all
the time deck and discover in the first round that it sucks ass, who am
I hurting by saving myself further embarassment?

> To give it your best shot in a poor situation (you could get lucky and
> sit in front of ANOTHER crap deck, or sit as the predator of the one
> deck who couldn't deal with you).

What if I don't care? I don't want to try anymore; I want to go get
something to eat, or go play some different game.

> The success or failure of V:TES will be based on sales in the retail
> outlets, NOT by booster draft tournaments for out-of-print sets.

If the White Wolf people see 10 people play in a V:TES tournament, that
sends a message different than 36 people play in a V:TES tournament, and
a bunch of people wanted to play and couldn't get in.

Another example: Shadowfist had an extremely good showing at GenCon.
That sends a message to the Shadowfist people that there is a large
interest in their game. Now they'll print more cards and spend more on
promotion, because they have a good indicator that it will pay off.

> But you know what? There really are a whole boatload of
> fucking losers playing Magic, as WELL as the decent, cultured,
> intelligent people. Why? I don't know. Just because you dislike the
> fact, and dislike that it gets brought up a lot, doesn't make it any
> less true, OR any less relevant.

Do you know what? There really are a whole boatload of fucking losers
playing V:TES. I'm not here as some defender of Magic or Magic people;
I do believe that, as card games go, it's not one of the best ones. But
you can't make generalizations like "most people who play Magic are
losers" and "most people who play V:TES aren't losers". I would go out
on a limb and say that a lot of people who play any CCG at all are
people who have a hard
time socializing with people in any other way. (Perhaps this is what
you mean by "losers.")

> And as such, the general public will form its opinions of the card
> game based on the most well-known one: Magic. And that's not serving
> as an especially good front-man right now, other than to show how CCGs
> can make shedloads of money off of gamers.

I'd actually have to say that the most well-known CCG at this point is
Pokemon. In which case the public's opinion of card game players is
that we're all 12 year old boys. ;)

> >is reasonable to expect someone to finish a game. It is reasonable to
> >expect someone to play _some_ part of a tournament that they enter. But
> >just because you think people should stay for the whole thing doesn't
> >mean you can make them do it, and it doesn't mean they should do it,
> >either.
>
> It doesn't mean that I can make them do it. But i'm afraid that
> committing to play in a 7-10 hour tournament -does- mean that one
> SHOULD stay for the full thing.

If, as I said before, the event description said: you will have to stay
for the entire event, then I would agree with you. But it didn't, and I
don't think it should have.

> >[If I get personally attacked again, this will be the last I say on the
> >subject. Note: "Your argument is unreasonable" is not a personal
> >attack. "You are a terrible person of low character" _is_ a personal
> >attack.]
>
> Fine. Please identify where I said you were a terrible person of low
> character?

That was someone else, and the statement was not directed at you
(sorry).

[snip: pool, losing on purpose better than just dropping out]

If I'm playing in a tournament, I'd rather play against someone who was
trying to win than someone who would just rather not be there. I don't
want to play against someone who is trying to lose; it's just no fun.
Why force someone to stay in a tournament if they don't want to be
there?

[N.B.: I'm not usually one who puts "smileys" in their messages, but I
wanted to emphasize that I'm not trying to sound angry or combative, but
that's hard to convey over text without things like ":)".]

fre...@netcom.com (Frederick Scott) wrote:
>
>
> X_Ze...@email.msn.com writes (about why resigning in a V:tES
tournament
> is unethical):
>
> >Certainly it is alright to resign in a game of Jyhad once it has
become
> >hopeless, but you do not quit out of a double elimination chess or
> >cricket tournament (may I remind you that VTES tourneys are
> >considered to be triple elimination). The reason for this is because
> >how you play influences who gets to the finals. It is extremely
unfair
> >to play the first round (especially if you are playing a intercept
deck
> >or a anarch revolt deck) and deprive someone of victory points, then
> >drop out and not deny victory points to the opponents that should be
> >playing you later in the tournament. I would agree with you if VTES
> >tourneys were single elimination, but as they are not, I do not.
>
> I'm not sure you have this analyzed very well. You do not "not deny
> victory points" to your later opponents.

You do one of two things in a VTES game when it is all said and done.
You either provide a victory point with your own ousting, or you deny
your predator a victory point by surviving (Sometimes you can even do
both). When you sweep a table and drop you are denying those victory
points to someone else who is continuing in the tournament by removing
those points from the overall pool of possible victory points that will
get you to the finals. When you get ousted and provide a victory point
to your predator and then drop, that is one more victory point that your
predator has access to that noones else can get in later rounds. When
you gain victory points and are then ousted, you do both you remove
victory points from the table that the person who was your predator
should have gotten in addition to the one he/she got from ousting you.

The tables just get
reshuffled
> and they get a different game than they would have gotten otherwise.

With one victory point less availible in the general pool of victory
points. So now instead of playing on a 5 person table, someone has to
play on a 4 person table. So even if they sweep the table they still
are one point short of any other player who sweeps the table on a five
person table. So in general, one person leaving a tournament
substancially affects victory conditions for at least four other players
per round.

> It's not like each round is fixed and if a person drops out of the
> tournament, those who would play against his position get an empty
seat
> and a free victory point.

As I said above, it is exactly opposite of what your train of thought
is. That victory point that you, the quitting player, represent is
lost for the remainder of the tournament. This creates an uneven
playing field.

> As an aside, that would be weird - show up at a 5-person table, find
> two people have dropped so you're playing a three-person game. I'd be
> mad about having to play the three-person game, never mind the
potential
> for two free victory points. And I suppose the predators of the
"empty
> chairs" would also get 6 free pool as well as their free VP as they
> started off? (What about the third guy? Or both the other guys if
one
> player got both empty seats as prey. Yuck!)

I really don't know where you got the above idea from, or how you
arrived there. Perhaps it was my mentioning of a 5 person finals where
two players dropped. It was still a five person final, but instead of
the five best, you had the three best and two substitutes for the people
who dropped.

> But this isn't what happens, of course.

I'm glad your erronious assumptions haven't led you so far off-track.

> So ethics based on such assumptions are not valid in real V:tES
tournaments. In reality, the quitters
leave
> and take their table positions and victory points and six pool reward
for
> ousting with them.

And when they leave they deny the victory points that they have won to
other players who would have won them without the quitter being in the
tournament, and also they deny others the victory point that they
would gain by ousting the quitter all the next rounds of the tournament

If they don't tell the judge before they go, he
has
> the headache of trying to move things around just before the next
round
> starts (so leaving without warning is a distinct trangression), but
the
> remaining players should be as challenged by the competition as those
who
> played against the quitter in earlier rounds.

But the remaining players have less victory points that they could win
because of the quitter withdrawing.

> In fact, if you assume the quitters had reason to leave and that
> reason was they their deck sucked (or their play or both) then future
> opponents actually get screwed by losing the opportunity to play them
> after the quitters' first round opponents got such a chance. That
kind
> of speculation gets pretty conjectural though, so is not worth
engaging
> in.

That kind of speculation is reality whether you like it or not. Each
player represents a victory point. If you bring a poor deck then you
should be a victory point for a player each round of the tournament, not
just the first.

Comments Welcome,
Norman S. Brown, Jr.
