Correct. And when you do not play, you don't do any of these things;
hence you do not affect the tournament for better or worse. You do
affect the rounds you play in; but since you might affect them in any
of these ways and since adding all of the possible results yields (times
chance of that result) a big null and since we can't make any predictions
about what a given player will do, it's all the same. As both you and
Dereki have pointed out, dropping out _will_ affect the tournament. But
the expected result is exactly the same so I don't see the point in making
a fuss over it.

>> The tables just get reshuffled and they get a different game than they
>> would have gotten otherwise.
>
>With one victory point less availible in the general pool of victory
>points. So now instead of playing on a 5 person table, someone has to
>play on a 4 person table. So even if they sweep the table they still
>are one point short of any other player who sweeps the table on a five
>person table. So in general, one person leaving a tournament
>substancially affects victory conditions for at least four other players
>per round.

Yes, there's one point which is not available. But there's also one less
person competing for it. So the expected result is the same. Granted,
a person may not be able to gain a five victory, but the four point victory
is correspondingly easier. And we also cannot even say that the effect of
dropping out will change a five person table to a four person. If there
were 21 players in the tournament, you would have one five-person and four
four-person tables out of necessity. If one person dropped out, the affect
_should_ be to reorganize the tables into four five-person tables and drop
one table (unless the judge is being lazy). So I think the problem here
is that you're analyzing all this stuff way too simplistically. And your
perception of the effect is just plain wrong.

>> As an aside, that would be weird - show up at a 5-person table, find
>> two people have dropped so you're playing a three-person game. I'd be
>> mad about having to play the three-person game, never mind the
>> potential for two free victory points. And I suppose the predators of the
>> "empty chairs" would also get 6 free pool as well as their free VP as they
>> started off? (What about the third guy? Or both the other guys if one
>> player got both empty seats as prey. Yuck!)
>
>I really don't know where you got the above idea from, or how you
>arrived there.

Because this is the only way a dropout would affect a tournament in
the manner you were talking about. To alter it substantially, a player
would have to leave his victory point _in_ the tournament but not
compete for it. (As delinated above.) Or he would have to (somehow,
I don't know how) compete for the victory point but not bring one to
the table. But this isn't what happens. He goes, his victory point
goes, the whole thing's a wash. I don't understand why this is intuitive
to you. But at least it should be clear to you after a fairly minimal
amount of analysis. This is not like (for instance) a round robin
tournament of sports teams where late round forfeits are unfair to a
team's early round competition that had to compete to get a win against
the team dropping out.

>> In fact, if you assume the quitters had reason to leave and that
>> reason was they their deck sucked (or their play or both) then future
>> opponents actually get screwed by losing the opportunity to play them
>> after the quitters' first round opponents got such a chance. That
>> kind of speculation gets pretty conjectural though, so is not worth
>> engaging in.
>
>That kind of speculation is reality whether you like it or not. Each
>player represents a victory point. If you bring a poor deck then you
>should be a victory point for a player each round of the tournament, not
>just the first.

The trouble is, if you bring a good deck to the tournmanet, you will win
victory points and take them away from your early round opponents. This
potential result exactly cancels out the chance that you will lose early
and provide a victory point to your early round opponents that they wouldn't
have otherwise receive. Unless your argument is that quitters all tend
to be bad players (or tend to be good players), the effect of quitting just
washes out. And if you are arguing one trend or another, I don't care.
Such chances seem too trivial to me to worry about. Let the people leave
who want to leave.

Fred

>Nope. Just the opposite. It creates no particular vacuumw. One game is

Because it's not true? There are ALWAYS tables which are "easier" to
play on due to weaker decks, and it's pretty much a given that many
decks at the tournament are going to have their antitheses present.
Let's run it through for a second.

Assume each player's overall skill and deck effectiveness can be
quantified from 1 to 5 (a vast simplification, but effective for our
purposes.) This would hold for most cases, except when the deck got
into a predator/prey relationship with the One Deck that would
completely hose them. We COULD suppose that every single deck there
has one other deck there that it absolutely doesn't want to face at
all, but for simplicity let's not because then this whole example gets
completely out of hand and offtrack.

So, let's say you have a table that looks like this: 5, 4, 2, 3, 4.
And a table that looks like this: 5, 1, 3, 5, 4. Assume prey is to
the right in the sequence.

It's doesn't take a genius to tell that the first table is going to be
much more evenly balanced than the second one. The best player there
is flanked on both sides by strong players and will have slow,
possibly rough going. The weakest player has the direct support of
the best player. From there on down, everyone is trying to take out a
stronger deck, so it's going to be very hard-fought all the way round.

The second table, on the other hand, is probably a sweep for the first
player. His predator is solid but will be held in check somewhat by
his grandpredator, his prey is just a target, and his grandprey is
going to be in bad shape as well. After two quick VPs and 12 pool
gained, any '5' should mop up the rest of the table.

Now suppose that player '1' gets depressed due to his rapid exit, and
drops out of the tournament. No other table in later rounds is going
to have the same sort of imbalance that one raw, unskilled newbie can
make - and nobody else will have such an easy chance of gaining 5 VPs
in a row. He also converted each round from a total of 10 VPs to a
total of 9, causing great pain for anyone at a 4-player table. This
VP removal, admittedly, is slightly magnified by our example using
only 10 players, but the person who swept the table is in excellent
shape with his 5 VPs and could probably slack off totally and still be
in the final - especially since everyone else has a much harder chance
of getting a 5 themselves after this.

By the same token, suppose that same 5-VP player gets bored and
leaves. His presence directly affected the other 4 players at his
table, and the other 5 players should have a chance to be equally
screwed. But they won't, because he's gone - those first 4 players
have got a zero that nobody else will have the same chance of getting.

>No. It's correct. A four-player game has four players competing for
>four points. A five-player game has five players competing for five
>points. Divide the points you get out of it by the number of players
>and the expected result - which is what's important - is still one.
>That's why tournaments have no problems sending some players to four
>player tables and others to five player tables. They don't even do
>anything about trying to balance who got sent to four and five player

>Because it's not important.

It is more important than you think. A person who is stuck at three
four-player tables has a maximum available VP of 12. A person who
plays at three five-player tables has a maximum available VP of 15.
In general, 6 VPs will get you into the final - the first person must
win half the VPs he sees. The second person must merely win
two-fifths - another significant difference.

There is a reason that the current tourney seating formula goes out of
its way to produce 5-player tables whenever possible, and also goes
out of its way to make sure people don't get repeatedly stuck on
4-player tables. That extra VP -will- begin to matter.

>I have no idea why these should be important or why you're obsessing over
>them. After you've quit, people can't gain YOUR victory point, sure. But
>they're given a correspondingly challenging victory point they could gain -

See above - if your deck blows a big hairy monkey, you have an
enormous effect on every table you sit at. (your prey gets a free
ride until your predator rolls over you.) If you bring weenie
dominate bleed from hell, and you hammer a table in 30 minutes, then
leave, you unfairly screw the other 4 players you played with. Decks
are not as random as all that to produce "equal" chances.

>(Except for Derek's arguments about the type of deck you bring, which I
>consider to be trivial, BTW.) A victory point is a victory point is a

You can claim they're 'trivial' all you want, but don't think that if

he should get to reshuffle his deck until he
gets a good start, because otherwise the next
two tables he sits at won't have gotten screwed
like his first table did? There's too much
randomness in Jyhad (even in tournaments) for
the 'dropouts skew the remaining player distribution
toward goodness/badness' argument to be plausible.

IMO, anyway.

> I happen to bring an incredibly weak deck that it won't sharply affect
> every table I'm at. If I then bail with that incredibly weak deck, I
> just boosted my original predator on a free ride to the finals. This
> is fair why?

Nothing's fair in card tournaments. Fairness
isn't even possible. To guarantee fairness
you'd have to remove the randomness, and then
it wouldn't be a card game anymore.

There's no guarantee that that original
predator, who your weak deck may have given
1 VP and 6 pool to, gets a free ride to
the finals. Maybe he gets bad draws his next
two rounds. Maybe he runs into an intercept-
untap deck after ousting you and gets no
more VPs in that first round. Maybe he just
had the anti-your-deck-deck and got to oust
you real quick but couldn't kill anyone else
in the entire tournament.

When people are allowed to be random factors
in (a) deck choice, (b) play skill, and (c)
in-game actions (how they vote or act or play
master cards, all of which may aid the other
players more in one game than another), why
should the line be drawn at allowing them to
be random factors in whether or not they play
in any particular round? We may castigate
people if we think they're throwing games, but
do we castigate them for playing inconsistently?
And if not, how can we castigate them for
dropping out early?

Josh

Fine. I don't care. This stuff is trivial and minor and in no
way should prevent people from worrying about leaving a tournament
if they need to leave. You are overly obsessing about how a change
in circumstances _may_ affect a tournament and ignoring the fact that
since it's difficult to say how it will affect the tournament, it
essentially doesn't mean anything.

By the same token, I could shuffle my deck before the start of a game
and pile my cards up in a way that will be cause me to totally lose
when I start to play the game due to a horribly unforunate ordering of
the cards. I don't know that, but it's true. Now I sit and look at
the face down pile and contemplate shuffling the cards for a second
time. If I do so, I'll likely affect the game and the tournament in
any number of ways. Do I care? No - because I have no idea what the
effect of a shuffle is going to be. This is the level of your objections
about people leaving tournaments (except to the extent of someone who
is aware that their deck is distinctly good or bad...see below). I don't
care about them, either, and neither should you.

>See above - if your deck blows a big hairy monkey, you have an
>enormous effect on every table you sit at. (your prey gets a free
>ride until your predator rolls over you.) If you bring weenie
>dominate bleed from hell, and you hammer a table in 30 minutes, then
>leave, you unfairly screw the other 4 players you played with. Decks
>are not as random as all that to produce "equal" chances.

It's true, if your deck sucks and you're a bad player, then you can make
some predictions about your effect on the future of the tournament,
though nothing is certain. By the same token, if you realize you're
God's gift to the game of Jyhad and you can usually expect to trash
the field, you can make some predictions about your effect as well.
Though again, even a Jyhad stud has no protection against chance and
the horrible shuffle. I concede this may be a basis for concern.

Notice, however, that the middle-of-the-road player may feel totally free
to leave, since he can make no predictions about his future performance.
To me, this just demonstrates how silly this whole line of argument is.
If you really felt this way, you should have asked Andrew and James
what they thought about their chances because this would become a relevant
question. I notice no one did. My conclusion is that none of you really
believe in your hearts that a dropout actually harms anyone to any great
extent. You're just obsessing over the fact that things are different
now, which is just about as important as the question of whether one more
shuffle of a totally randomized deck makes a difference.

Fred

The reason those points would be better off is that they are points that
would have been availible to other players. So now the final point score
is skewed because you left with points that should have gone to other
players who intended to finish the tournament. The points you won on
the table should have been won by someone else in your absence, and the
point that your potential ousting represents in the rounds you
did not participate is also denied to other players. So now by leaving
you have "screwed" the other players out of those points.

I am sorry that you can not conceptualize the impact of empty points on
the tournament, but that is what the above mentioned points are, empty.
By quitting you negate the value of those points. To use an analogy, It
is like taking burning U.S. Currency. The currency has a value, which
is only good for exchange, but you are destroying it, therefore taking
it out of circulation. The U.S. government expects a fixed supply of
money to be availible, and bases all of its calculations on that fixed
supply (calculations like taxes). Only now you have reduced that fixed
amount, therefore rendering their calculations erroneoous. There is a
reason that destroying currency is against the law. It is a bad thing
because it messes up the money supply. For example if the overall money
supply is $1,000,000.00 and you burn $100,000.00, then you now only have
$900,000.00. The government expects there to be $1,000,000.00 in
circulation. So, the government taxes its citizens for $300,000.00, but
now there is only $900,000.00. So instead of paying a tax rate of 30%
you are now paying a tax rate of 33%. This is a real world example of
why removing currency from circulation is la crime.

Similarly, quitting a tournament messes up the points supply. Points
are used to get to the finals in tournaments. If you quit, then you
remove points from the point supply. These points would have been there
if you had never participated, but you, the quitter, quit and therefore
wrecked the points distribution for the tournament.

So, if your mentality is that you don't wreck the points spread by
removing yourself from a tournament, then you obviously don't see how
removing them from circulation affected the overall point distribution.
In saying that, you are saying that if you started burning cash (thereby
removing money from the money supply) then your taxes wouldn't increase.
The money would become more valuable and therefore your lump sum of
taxes to the government would be worth more.

Similarly when you remove yourself from a tournament, the remaining
points in the tournament become more valuable because there are less to
be had. So if you won alot of points in the first round your points are
more valuable now that a player has quit. Conversely, if you won no
points in the first round and a player quits, you are screwed. Points
become scarcer and the players with a larger win in rounds prior to the
quitter quitting are better off than players who win points after the
quitter has quitted.

Do you now understand how quitting screws up the point spread or do I
have to break out charts and graphs?

Oh no. No no no. This is not an accurate
economic picture.

If, instead of burning $100,000 of the $1,000,000
money supply, you stuck it all in your mattress,
and never spent it in your life, would that be a
crime? No, it wouldn't. Why not? Because when
you have money, you can do whatever you want with
it. The law against destroying currency is mostly
just because the government likes to tell you what
to do.

If you *did* take your $100,000 out of circulation,
by burning it, stuffing all your pillows with it,
or whatever, that would *not* make the effective
tax rate higher.

The remaining $900,000 would now be 'worth' what
the previous $1,000,000 was 'worth'. Taking money
out of circulation is deflationary: it causes nominal
prices to fall. Things that used to cost $1.00 will
now cost $0.90.

If the government *did* decide to tax people for
$300,000 of their wealth (what it thought was a
30% wealth tax), that would indeed become a 33%
wealth tax after the $100,000 was taken out of
circulation. But governments don't usually tax
wealth, for this among other reasons. Instead
they usually tax income, and they tax it at some
fixed percentage rate. If the government had an
income tax beforehand of 30% of everyone's annual
income, and it was expecting people to have
$1,000,000 in income, it would have expected to get
$300,000. After the $100,000 left circulation,
people's income would be $900,000 for the year, and
the government's 30% tax would take $270,000 of
that, which brings us right back to the government
getting 30% of the total income in the economy.

As you can see, taking money out of circulation
*does not* change anything about the 'real' size
of the economy (that is, the amount of goods and
services produced). It changes only the numbers
attached to those goods and services, which is to
say, the 'nominal' size of the economy.

Make sense?

> Similarly, quitting a tournament messes up the points supply. Points
> are used to get to the finals in tournaments. If you quit, then you
> remove points from the point supply. These points would have been
there
> if you had never participated, but you, the quitter, quit and
therefore
> wrecked the points distribution for the tournament.

Just like in an actual economy, it doesn't matter
if you take your first-two-rounds ten victory points
and go home with them. Instead of you being top seed
in the finals, the person with the next-highest VP
total will be top seed. As long as there are at least
five people remaining in the tournament, there will
be people to take all the seats in the finals.

By ousting people instead of being ousted by them,
you have made it harder for certain individuals to
get to the finals. However, that's exactly what
would have happened to them if you *had* stayed in
the tournament and played in the finals - they would
be no less screwed if you did *not* drop than if you
do.

> So, if your mentality is that you don't wreck the points spread by
> removing yourself from a tournament, then you obviously don't see how
> removing them from circulation affected the overall point
distribution.
> In saying that, you are saying that if you started burning cash
(thereby
> removing money from the money supply) then your taxes wouldn't
increase.
> The money would become more valuable and therefore your lump sum of
> taxes to the government would be worth more.

But the money you have left would *also* be worth
more! Plus, the government *doesn't tax people* in
lump-sum terms. It's all in percentages, partially
because the government *doesn't know* what the money
supply is.

> Similarly when you remove yourself from a tournament, the remaining
> points in the tournament become more valuable because there are less
to
> be had. So if you won alot of points in the first round your points
are
> more valuable now that a player has quit. Conversely, if you won no
> points in the first round and a player quits, you are screwed. Points
> become scarcer and the players with a larger win in rounds prior to
the
> quitter quitting are better off than players who win points after the
> quitter has quitted.

This isn't right either.

If a no-points player leaves the tournament after
the first round, there will be two fewer VPs total
to be distributed among all the players. However,
there are also two fewer player-spots trying to win
VPs. Every player's "expected VPs each round"
(that is, the statistical average number of VPs each
player would win over an infinite number of rounds)
remains the same: 1.

There are fewer VPs to be won, yes, but it will
now require fewer VPs to make the finals!

The only thing that keeps Jyhad tournaments from
adhering perfectly to these principles is that
the scoring system is relatively granular: there
are not that many discrete levels of VPs for
different players to have. This is because the
expected score each round is only 1, rather than,
say, 10 or 100, and there are no fractional VPs
(except for time-outs). In bowling, for example,
your score could range from 0 to 300 for a single
game. In Jyhad, it can only range from 0 to 5.
Since there are fewer possible levels, you may
end up with more ties if people with lots of VPs
do drop out before the finals. In practice, though,
I think people with many VPs are much less likely
to drop out than people with few or no VPs.

> Do you now understand how quitting screws up the point spread or do I
> have to break out charts and graphs?

I apologize for being blunt, but I'm not sure that
*you* understand how quitting does (or doesn't)
screw up the point spread.

Josh "Economist" Duffin

the fact that there are OTHERS in the world too - and also no

creating a good draft deck than the guys on the next table who may all
be competing for the effective cards and largely passing up the precious
ones.) But I've seldom seen it have a major effect on a tournament
because the rare cards are just that: rare. They only affect things
once in a while.

If it's really that important, I guess you could do something like
redraft cards at the end of the tournament (good incentive to keep
players in the tournament, too) and give the best performing players
the first pick - or even more picks. There's some distinct inconveniences
in something like that, however. My suspicion is that most players
would just prefer the imperfection of allowing the stripmining. Given
that point, let the stripminers stripmine and don't moralize about it.
There's no point that I can see.

Fred

Sure. But so does an extra shuffle. If you show up at a tournament,
everything you do, every card you play, every deck you cut, every

players to play to win the games they start to the best of their non-cheating

how they'll affect anything (e.g. one more shuffle), there's no point
in worrying about them. So it is with the player who owns 0-VP deck
deciding whether to quit or not.

Here is where I would disagree with you. There are less points
availible in the third round than in the first. Often this comes in the
form of a 4 person table being created or a six-person table being
eliminated. Now here is were the problems begin. If you get put on the
4 person table, you can sweep the table but you gain one less point than
a person who sweeps a five player table. On the other hand if you get
put on a six person table, rather than being able to sweep the whole
table because of the two hour time limit, the table will normally time
out or be split between two players.

Now if the tournament started with an odd table, usually a person
quitting will either eliminate the odd table (in the case of the odd
table being a six player table) or create more odd tables (in the case
of the odd table being a four person table). If you eliminate the odd
table, then the people who had to play on the odd table have had to play
in a more difficult circumstance than the players on the standard
table. The other option is if multiple odd table are created, this is
normally in the form of six player tables which are more difficult to
play on.

> I guess the problem here is that you're using a model for thinking
about
> this which has nothing to do with reality.

The problem with my model is that is uses decimals and fractions, but
what happens in a tournament is that all those decimals and fractions
add up and "land" at a table. This "landing" at a table comes in the
form of a odd table being created or disbanded. The appearance or
disappearance of the odd table is what screws up the points spread.

If we were spending our
points
> on fabulous prizes at the end of the tournament, then there'd be some
> kind of effect, I suppose. But that doesn't happen.

But we are spending our points, we are spending them to purchase a seat
in the finals. The price of that seat fluctuates with the number of
players. The more players that enter into a tournament the more points
it requires to get into the finals. In a small tournament (12 to 15
players) normally 4 victory points will get you into the finals where as
in a large tournament (30+ players) it requires 6 victory points to
guarantee a spot in the finals. It is a simple supply and demand curve.
Five seats are the fixed supply curve and the demand curve varies based
on the number of players in the tournament.

I hope this help.

>$1,000,000 in income, it would have expected to get
>$300,000. After the $100,000 left circulation,

> Six-player tables are not supported at V:EKN tournaments: all tables
are to
> be four- or five-player tables. [VEKN 3.1.2]

Thanks.
So a twenty-one person tournament is 4 tables of 4 and one table of 5
instead of 3 tables of 5 and one of six. So now if a person drops the
seating goes to 4 tables of 5. Now the players on the single initial
table of 5 have a potential advantage over the tables of 4 because they
had the potential to win 5 victory points where everyone else only had
the potential to win 4 victory points. So in effect, a player dropping
out of the tournament has just penalized 16 players. Now, your counter
to this may be that those sixteen players would be penalized the length
of the entire tournament, but in reality what the judge would do is
rotate 5 new players to the 5 player table each round. So if 5 players
each round sit at the the five player table for three rounds that is
fifteen players who have access to an addition victory point, leaving 6
players without access to the additional victory point, as opposed to
having someone quit after the first round which denies 16 players access
to an additional victory point. So by quitting you have denied and
additional 10 players access to an additional victory point.

I was going to put a big chart in here that would have shown the
distribution of victory point across the tables, and how changing the
number of players aversely affects the the sixteen players in one round
versus six over the course of the tournament, but instead I think I can
explain it with out the chart.

In the first round you have 4 tables of players with access to 4
victory points for each table and one table with access to 5 victory
points. If no one drops out of the tournament players are rotated on
and off the table with 5 victory point. Being seated at the table with
5 victory points is an advantage because you have the potential to sweep
and gain one more victory point than if you swept on a 4 person table.
So you have three rounds with 5 people each round get the opportunity to
gain a extra victory point for a total of 15 people getting the
opportunity, and the six players who did not get the opportunity to gain
an extra victory point.

Now if a person drops after the first round and the tables are reset to
3 tables of 5 players each, now all the players for the remainder of the
tournament (barring another person quitting) have access to 5 points
each round for the remainder of the tournament. Unfortunantly since
everyone now is on a level playing field, the 5 players at the 5 person
in the first round table enjoyed an advantage that was not availible to
other 16 players during that round of a tournament. That advantage was
the opportunity to score one more victory point for a sweep. From
past experience, I have seen that it is often one victory point that
separates the 5th seat (i.e. the player making it with the lowest
point score) in the finals from the next runner up. So this puts 16
players at a potential disadvantage to the 5 players who had the
opportunity to score 5 points.

How the advantage works is shown in both the sweep scenario and the
split scenario. These scenarios are based on identical performance
on a four person table and a five person table.

The sweep scenario is that you sweep the entire table and score all the
victory points. Obviously, it is to your advantage to be sitting on a
table with more potential victory points (i.e the 5 person table rather
than the 4 person table) in this scenario.

In the split scenario, on a four person table there are two ways the
points can be split. Those two ways are 1-3, 1-1-2 or 2-2. This is
versus a five person table where the split is 1-4, 2-3, 1-1-1-2, 2-2-1,
1-1-3. So you will see that on a four person there are only 3 possible
ways to split victory point versus a five player table where there is
five possible ways to split victory points. Given identical
performances a player has a better chance of walking away from a five
person table with a victory point as there are more ways to gain one
(i.e. the potential to gain an additional victory point).

Hope this helps.

Well, I think I can see where you were coming

Counting up ways to split VPs is not a useful
way to analyze 'chances of getting a VP'. If
you want to assume that every outcome is equally
likely and then calculate the likelihood of
each different outcome, like when you're figuring
probabilities of different numbers when rolling
dice, you can do that. But you need a (much)
longer list: for example, there are five ways
just to get the 5-0-0-0-0 split, and twenty ways
to get the 4-1-0-0-0 split. There are so many
ways to get the 2-2-1-0-0 split that I don't even
want to count them. (I know there's a formula
to figure out how many there are without counting,
but I don't remember it.)

Anyway. If you're trying to figure out the
average number of victory points each person
will get, assuming that who gets how many each
game is random, it's easy: each person will
average one (1) VP. This is because there always
exists (except for timeouts) one VP per player.
This is why the four-table disadvantage is not
a *huge* disadvantage: yes, the most VPs you can
get on a four-player table is 4, whereas you
could get 5 on a five-player table. But *on
average* you would get only 1 on either.

Would you argue that 20-player tables would
give you a better chance to walk away from
the table with a victory point than 5-player
tables? The same argument as the one you
presented for 4 vs 5 holds. But in fact,
you get a VP by ousting the person to your
left before the person to your right ousts
you. It doesn't matter how many people are
on the table: your average VPs from a game
is always one.

It's true that the maximum possible VPs from
a game goes up with more players. But the
larger numbers are less and less likely as
the table gets bigger. (Not to mention that
larger tables are more likely to time out,
in which case VPs are lost and no one gets to
sweep.)

Also: in your scenario above, if the player
drops, fifteen players have 'access' to 14
total VPs and five have 'access' to 15. If
he does not drop, six players have 'access'
to 12 VPs and fifteen have 'access' to 13.
Is it really clear that this is more equitable?

As for one VP being the difference between
making the finals and not - perhaps you have
been playing in larger tournaments than me,
but I have seen many more cases where the
fourth, fifth, and sixth-ranked players are
separated by no more than half a VP if that,
and who goes to the finals is determined by
the tournament-points tiebreaker. And in
tournaments like that, one sweep is generally
enough to get you to the finals, whether it's
on a four-player or five-player table.

Josh

LSJ was fairly frosty when I told him that I was dropping out of the
Sabbat event. I explained why and repeated my comments here.

Anyway, I advise against giving someone a hard time if they say that
they are leaving. For one thing, this would just encourage them to go
away without telling anyone.

I often run Shadowfist draft/sealed deck events at game conventions.
These are a bargain in monetary terms but I still encourage fringe
players to join in on a casual basis. It's better to get them to
sample the game and let it sell itself than to fret over the extent to
which they will take part. If they have other interests or
commitments, I can readily appreciate that and will still welcome them
back later.

The thing that people seem to be obsessing about here are the demands
of the three-round + final format. Looking at the VEKN rules, I see
that they require a minimum of 2 preliminary rounds of 2 hours each.
This means that a single elimination format is not possible - that's a
shame as that seems a good format for players with limited time to
spare.

One thing I don't understand is what's supposed to happen in the third
qualifying round if a player has scored no VP at this point and can be
certain that they will not make the final. It seems very wrong that
such players should play alongside players who are still in contention
- they can only act as king-makers. The VEKN rules don't seem to
address this but I would expect it to become a big deal if you ever
did get large numbers of players for an event.

Andrew

>availible in the third round than in the first. Often this comes in the
>form of a 4 person table being created or a six-person table being
>eliminated.

In a large enough tournament, there should be nothing but four and five-
person tables. No matter. As I've already pointed out to you, it's as
easy to get a victory point on a four-person table as a five-person table.

>Now here is were the problems begin. If you get put on the
>4 person table, you can sweep the table but you gain one less point than
>a person who sweeps a five player table.

And, since you have only three opponents, sweeping the table is
correspondingly easier on a four-person table. This is why judges do
not take pains to equalize competition on four vs. five person tables.

And also, assuming one type of table were easier to win points on than
another, then dropping out *still* doesn't cause a problem because one
has a 20% chance of causing the drop of an entire table and creating
four five-person tables out of four four-person tables and an 80% chance
of reducing the size of one five-person table to four-people. This is
statistically a wash: the person has overall the same chance of increasing
a table size as decreasing one. It's not important but it should eliminate
and remaining problems you would have with the "table size" issue.

>> If we were spending our points on fabulous prizes at the end of the
>> tournament, then there'd be some kind of effect, I suppose. But that
>> doesn't happen.
>
>But we are spending our points, we are spending them to purchase a seat
>in the finals.

BZZZZZT!!!!! Wrong answer. You do not spend points in any way, shape,
or form. You simply accumulate them and you receive the seat by being the
person with one of the top five totals. This doesn't work the same way
as a monetary system that has inflation, deflation, commodity vales, etc.

None the less, I can see what you're getting at: if there's less points
in the system, it requires fewer points to make the finals. That may well
be true, particularly if someone sweeps two tables and quits in the third
round. None the less, it does *not* cause unfairness.

Keep in mind that the tournament is a contest for victory points. In order
to be fair, all that's important is that all the players have an equally
difficult time winning them. It isn't necessary for purposes of fairness
that it be equally difficult to win them in each round - recall game shows
where the points in the first round are usually pretty meaningless,
increased significantly in the second round, and some single dramatic
contest in the final round usually decides the victor (the show's sponsors
need that!). Still, a Jyhad tournament is designed to be that way so we'll
assume it's important.

So I ask you, if I have to face a table full players in the first OR third
round, what's the difference if the tournament is missing a table or two?
Not a damn thing!

Fred

Unforunately, that's the problem. That is not an advantage since you
are incorrect that sitting at a five person table is an advantage. It's
true that you're theorectical maximum points in a five-player game is
higher but that's not the only consideration. Consider the fact also
that it's harder to sweep a five-player table. After ousting three
opponents, you may still be ousted ousted by the fourth. Or that you
may be near ousting your prey and starting the sweep, but there's one more
person in the game who may beat you to the punch and start rolling up
your opponents before you start your sweep.

game. There's ALSO five players! It's not like someone came along and
threw and extra VP in without the corresponding challenge.

seventeen players - leaving two people relatively screwed. Instead,

supposed to be worse? How did you figure out that 15 out of 17 is good

Chinese

out

I always thought that in tournaments, everyone was
supposed to bring a killer deck? I mean, for sure,

VPs you got in your last game than of how well
your deck is performing in this game? If so, I
have to think they're not playing the game well.
It's not to your advantage to give someone else

very little indeed. The actual VP is worth
a lot. But the "chance" to get one more VP

Well, average points per table is an interesting statistic except that I
have never seen any table score exactly one point per player, and
the only time I have seen the possibility in the 12 tournaments I have
played of it even occuring was in this past tournament in New Orleans.
The occurence that almost caused it was a domain challenge being called
on the table that would have ousted everyone (including the player who
called it). Of course, it was voted down immediately ,because unless you
are about to be ousted, you try to score as many victory points as
possible, and scoring only one victory point while being ousted just
like everyone else on the table is not a viable victory stratagy to get
you into the finals.

Also, to address average points per player, do you build your
tournament decks to merely score the average amount of points? I don't,
and I honestly believe that most other players don't either. What you
want is the most points. It is more likely that you will get more
points if you have access to more possible points than other players.
If I have access to 15 points, and you only have access to 12 points,
then I can win a smaller percentage of the points I have availible to me
than you can and still make it to the finals before you. And maybe,
make it to the finals instead of you because although as hard as you
tried you just didn't get a the same chance I did.

Although, I can see why it doesn't matter to players who voluntarily
quit whether they score enough points to make it to the finals or not,
because they never intended to get to the finals in the first place.
They are playing for a whole different set of reasons. Reasons I don't
understand. Perhaps the fun is in quitting, I don't know.

possible detriment of the judge and players. If you want to "have a right to

I have 2 items and get stuck behind the full grocery cart I'm stuck. Why?

grocery cart was there first and that is fair. If I'm in front, others have
to wait for me. That is also fair. Why? Because the store, and society in
general, says the person in line first gets severed first. Why is it
suddenly different when it comes to the rules and fairness of a tournament?
If I applied your logic in regards to VTES tournaments to this example I

You said (above) "do you have the right ...? No." How is that a correct
statement?

> However it is interesting to note there is a penalty if not announced. If
> withdrawl is no problem why the penalty?

Unannounced withdrawal is a problem, since it requires the TO to reseat
the round, which can be a hassle. However, if the TO is notified
properly, there really isn't a problem; you'll have to do the same
amount of work seating the round, you just toss away one of your index
cards (or whatever).

> I would still make the point that dropping out is not intended to be part of
> the tournament.

Well, consider that the V:EKN tournament rules are based on the DCI
tournament rules, which are based on the DCI tournament rules for
Magic. And in Magic (as in every other card game I've ever heard of),
dropping part-way through a tournament is acceptable.

Look: I'm sick of arguing the "morality" of dropping out. Clearly you
feel very passionately on the subject. As much as I disagree with you,
you're always going to harbor animosity towards people who drop from a
tournament. The point I'm trying to make is that this is _your_
problem. Just because you don't like it doesn't mean it shouldn't be
permitted. You (or someone like you) have already agreed that it would
be nearly impossible to keep people from dropping voluntarily. By
making such a huge deal out of this, what happens to casual players who
would like to play in tournaments but don't necessarily want to stick
around getting their butts kicked the whole time? They're not going to
understand why you want them to stay (I sure don't), and your attitude
may very well sour them on the whole tournament experience. My opinion
is that we could use as many people playing in tournaments at major
events as possible. If some of them drop, people aren't going to think
"what a crappy game, people dropped out so it must be crappy". If they
play _any_ other card game, they will be aware that people drop out of
tournaments. It doesn't mean the game sucks; it means they were doing
crappy, and since they drove hundreds of miles to get to a friggin'
convention, they're not about to sit around not having fun while there's
200 other fun things to be doing.

As I write this, I'm imagining all the counter-arguments being brought
up _again_ and wonder why I even bother. So, if anyone has anything
else new to say on the matter, please do... otherwise, I'm just too sick
of this thread to bother anymore.

James

Whatever. This is a different argument. There _are_ 2 or 3 rounds and a

These things are the domain of the tournament rules. Generally speaking,
if you violate something in the tournament rules, you are saddled with a

makes it more difficult for you to win the tournament. Some rules may

tournament before finishing. If there were such a commitment as you're
trying to suggest, then one would expect to see a tournament rule involving

the VEKN rules (for example), merely state that they "must inform the

scorekeeper before the seatings for the next round are generated".

risk receiving no victory points (but presumedly being show as participating
in the game, which I case penalizes their rating) for the next round.

I think you do what they did with the Superbowl. (It was actually halftime

is causing a problem, you make a special appeal to the players not to
engage in it, which is limited to when and where the problem occurs. You

the finals, you'd have to sweep three five-player tables - in which case
playing on a four-player table would be the kiss of death. But if they

just one.

Okay, where the hell did that come from?

Governments do not, in general, have pre-existing
expenses that they have to pay for independent of
tax revenue. They collect taxes and spend money
throughout any given fiscal year.

Bringing 'foreign loans' into the picture is just
silly. (1) what is the analogy to Jyhad; (b) why
do you want to bring foreign countries into a nice
simple one-country economic model; (iii) what kind
of government would have all its tax revenue committed
to 'foreign loans'?

> Also, in the case of tournament play, when someone drops out it
doesn't
> decrease the value of the already gained VP's among the other players.
> With your example 5 VP's would have become 4.5 VP's but they're still5
> VP....which is what this whole discussion is about! Those who earned 5
> VP's are suddenly "richer" than they would have been if the player
> stayed. I don't see why you can't admit that there's a significant

That's not what I said.

In my example, if someone with no VPs drops out
of a tournament after the first round, there
will be two fewer VPs gained by all players
collectively (VPs in the "economy") than if the
player had stayed in.

However, there will also be two fewer player-
spots competing for VPs at the second and third
round tables.

Fewer VPs in the economy means that each remaining
VP is "worth" more: it will take fewer VPs to
qualify for the final round.

If a player with several VPs after the first round
drops out of the tournament, there will be, after
the third round, X+2 VPs less among the players still
in the tournament, where X is the number he or she
had after the first round. Again, there are fewer
VPs in the "economy" so the VPs of the people still
in the tournament are more "valuable", and it will
take even fewer VPs to qualify for the final round.

What my entire economics discussion was meant to
show is that, when an economy "shrinks", the "money"
remaining in the economy is "worth" more in "real"
terms (ie, the same nominal amount of money, or VPs,
buys more than it did when there was more money, or
VPs, in the economy).

Thus, the only effect of a player dropping out of
a tournament on VP distribution is that it will
take fewer VPs to qualify for the finals. My
point is not that this effect doesn't exist, but
that it is insignificant, because if the player
*didn't* drop out, the five people with the highest
VP totals would *still* qualify for the finals.
It's just that those highest VP totals might not
be as high in nominal terms, since there are fewer
VPs in the economy.

Almost every country in the world has foreign loans that they have to
pay off on (at least the interest rate, unless they want the debt to
increase even further) and for this matter the government needs a
budget. There can be thousands of scenarios as to why the governemnt

If there's 5 spots for the final, and you happen to be #6 and trying to
get enough VP's to make it to the final, you will try figure out how
many points you need to get. If someone who doesn't have a chance to
make it to the final drops out, then that means you lose the
opportunity to get a VP by ousting him. It could be that very VP you
needed to pass the current #5 player and make it to the final. It's not
at all eaiser to make it to the final because someone dropped, in this
case. If the dropper never had a chance to make it to the final, then
his absence doesn't make the competition less, it in fact makes it even
harder to reach the final, because there's one less VP to gain, and as
the #6 you need as many as you can get.

This is the same inaccurate logic that's been addressed
several times already in this thread. I'll try to
explain my perspective once more, but after that I don't
think there's any point in going on.

If you are #6 after two preliminary rounds and someone
drops, you will still have someone sitting next to
you in the third round that you can oust to get to the
finals. The worst thing that can happen to you is that
the drop might cause there to be one more four-player
table than there was before the drop, and you could sweep
that four-player table but not make it to the finals
because you needed five points to make it and only got
four.

However, you could have been randomly seated at a
four-player table even if that player had *not*
dropped. You would have been equally out of luck.
Furthermore, for you to have been #6 after two rounds
and still #6 after three rounds after getting 4 VPs,
everyone in the first five places would have to have
gotten 5 VPs. An unlikely scenario, to say the least.

Also note that the player who left and is no longer
available to be ousted is *also* no longer trying
to oust anyone. If he stayed in and ousted exactly
one person, that would *still* be a VP that you could
not get, and if he was not in contention for the
finals that VP would be just as much "lost" as if he
had dropped out. If he stayed in and *withdrew from
the game*, he would keep his VP and you would still
not be able to get it. Would you describe these
scenarios as "increasing competition"?

This is why I see the effects of a dropout in a large
tournament as negligible at worst and unmeasurable at
best. You don't "lose the opportunity to gain a VP
by ousting him" because there will be someone *else*
sitting at your table who you have the substituted
opportunity to gain a VP by ousting. Only when a
five-player table becomes a four-player table is an
"opportunity" lost. And when a four-player table
becomes a five-player table, an "opportunity" is
instead gained (eg when a player drops from a 21-player
tourney - before, there were four four-player tables
and one five-player; after, there are four five-player
tables).

Josh
